title: Season over for Kangaroos AFLW star after spinal fusion surgery
text:
Two-time AFLW premiers North Melbourne have lost midfielder Mia King for the season after she required spinal fusion surgery for a neck injury.

The premiership midfielder reported neck pain following North's win over Brisbane Lions last weekend.

King underwent a thorough medical examination in Brisbane, which revealed a disc injury near her spinal cord.

She remains in Queensland recovering after having successful surgery to fuse together the C5 and C6 vertebrae in her neck.

Roos dominate Aussie AFLW squad North Melbourne has the most players of any club selected in Australia's squad for the inaugural AFLW representative match against Ireland.

The Kangaroos confirmed the procedure would sideline King for the rest of the 2026 season.

"We will continue monitoring Mia in her recovery but we don't expect this type of surgery to stop her from returning to play in 2027," club doctor Victoria Norbury said in a statement.

King was part of North Melbourne's premiership-winning team in 2024, but she missed out on last year's grand final win after an ongoing PCL knee injury.

The Kangaroos are again at the top of the ladder after two rounds this season, with the best percentage in the AFLW.

North Melbourne general manager of women's football Erin Lorenzini said the club would support King as she began her recovery.

"We wrap our arms around Mia," Lorenzini said. "We are devastated for her, but also full of admiration for how incredibly strong she has been this week.

"As a proud Jawoyn woman, she was particularly looking forward to wearing our Indigenous Round jumper in Launceston this weekend.

"We have a very close group of players and staff, and all our thoughts will be with her as we run out against the Bulldogs on Saturday."

title: Bathla workers stood down as company struggles to stay afloat
text:
Staff of major property developer Bathla group have been stood down as the company struggles to stay afloat.

It follows the NSW government knocking back a request from the company's administrators for financial support.

The Bathla Group fell into voluntary administration earlier this week, unable to pay debts that topped $3.2 billion.

The administrators stood down staff at the property developer's headquarters on Friday as the firm sought an urgent cash injection of $40 million to see it through until the end of September.

A spokesman for the NSW government said administrators made approaches to it for assistance.

"The government does not yet have a complete picture of the company’s financial position," the spokesman said.

" Given the circumstances, we are not willing to put taxpayers' money on the line to guarantee profits for private creditors. "

Court's quest for justice on white-collar crime Corporate regulator ASIC, and its new boss, is keeping a close watch on Australia's "permissive investment regime".

Several private credit firms have lent money to the developer, some of which have now limited investor redemptions.

About 2,000 homes are under construction across the group, and about 13,000 more are in its development pipeline.

Bathla is one of Sydney's most prolific residential developers, particularly across the city's west.

The company blamed a "perfect storm" of conditions for its collapse, including softening home sales, the federal government's property tax changes and high costs.

title: ICAC finds NSW Health director who faked CV 'seriously corrupt'
text:
A former senior NSW Health employee will be referred to the Director of Public Prosecutions after he was found to have engaged in serious corruption, including faking his CVs and nepotism.

In a report published on Friday, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) found Zoran Ribicic engaged in serious corrupt conduct over many years.

Mr Ribicic was the NSW Health director of engineering and asset management between 2021 and 2024.

ICAC claimed Mr Ribicic improperly awarded hundreds of thousands of taxpayers' dollars to external contractors, including his sister Mirela Derrin's company Risk Control Consulting (RCC), which received more than $275,000 in payments from Illawarra Shoalhaven Local Health District (ISLHD) across a two-year period.

ICAC found he also favoured RCC over competitors and never declared the conflict of interest to ISLHD.

Wollongong Hospital, which is part of the Illawarra Shoalhaven Local Health District. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

An ISLHD officer reported Mr Ribicic to ICAC in July 2024, and he was subsequently suspended with pay before he resigned in September that year.

Corruption exposed

Mr Ribicic was also found to have engaged in "order splitting", according to the ICAC report.

He was authorised to approve quotes up to $30,000, and requested favoured suppliers to break much larger bodies of work into bundles below that amount.

This allowed him to engage his family and associates without the competition and oversight that would ordinarily apply to substantial contracts.

ICAC Commissioner Helen Murrell presided over Zoran Ribicic's matter. (Supplied: ICAC)

Mr Ribicic told ICAC there were six critical maintenance issues that required attention after the COVID-19 pandemic.

These ranged from malfunctioning lifts and automatic doors to "having to shut down operating theatres because of condensation because cooling and, and, and ventilation wasn't good enough".

NSW ICAC Commissioner Helen Murrell said Mr Ribicic's lack of qualifications to resolve these maintenance issues could have threatened the safety of patients.

"He was not qualified to deal with these problems," she said.

" The things that happened may well be because the whole thing was being managed by somebody who wasn't qualified to do so. "

Mr Ribicic also deliberately failed to declare secondary employment with engineering and consulting firm Lanmar between 2023 and 2024, as required by ISLHD's code of conduct.

He received $210,375 for 10 months' work with the private company that he previously brought on as a consultant to ISLHD.

Alleged fraud

ICAC's report states Mr Ribicic will be referred to the DPP to consider potential fraud offences after he made six job applications to government departments.

These applications contained fake qualifications and used false references to land public sector roles between 2012 and 2025.

He falsely stated he had a doctorate in business administration, a master's degree in project management, a bachelor's degree in engineering and a TAFE Engineering diploma.

ISLHD and five other employers all failed to detect his dishonesty and hired him over a decade.

Public agencies to receive training

ICAC Commissioner Helen Murrell said the explosive findings carry several lessons for organisations to reduce risk of corruption in the workplace.

The recommendations in the report include stronger qualification verification processes, improved conflict of interest controls, enhanced procurement oversight, and improve governance arrangements for consultants.

She said ICAC would deliver training to public agencies like NSW Health in the coming months.

"We'll be leveraging off this report to deliver education to numerous agencies across New South Wales," she said

" It's more important to educate these agencies so that this doesn't happen again or at least the risk of it is minimised. "

Commissioner Murrell would not comment on whether there were any pending ICAC investigations into Mr Ribicic's dealings at the other companies where he was previously employed, but said some of his actions may result in criminal charges.

She lauded processes within the ISLHD that led to the corruption being reported to ICAC.

"It's really great when agencies suspect corrupt conduct and they report it to us," the commissioner said.

"What we worry about is when the internal processes of an agency are such that suspected corrupt conduct is not reported to us, but it's a statutory requirement for it to be reported to us, and that is what happened here."

ISLHD has been contacted for comment.

title: Elon Musk's rocket heads home to US after Christmas Island sojourn
text:
SpaceX's Starship 40 rocket has begun the long journey home after being retrieved from waters off Christmas Island.

Carrying the precious cargo, heavy duty transport vessel Forte departed the island on Friday afternoon, headed for the United States.

A snorkeller unperturbed by the SpaceX rocket nearby. (Supplied: Extra Divers Australia)

The rocket splashed down in the Indian Ocean on July 24, and spent just over three weeks at sea before being towed to Christmas Island, about 1,500 kilometres off Western Australia's northern coast.

The rocket was retrieved after 24 days at sea and towed to Christmas Island. (Supplied: SpaceX )

The Forte arrived in Flying Fish Cove last Sunday night, with the delicate operation to retrieve the rocket getting underway on Tuesday.

The vessel's ballast tank was filled with water to change the buoyancy of the ship, lowering its deck below the surface.

The rocket was positioned over the Forte with the help of locals before the vessel refloated. (Supplied: Paul Hollier)

Local stevedores assisted in the operation to position the rocket over the Forte before the vessel refloated, lifting the SpaceX cargo out of the water for the first time in more than a month.

Locals farewell SpaceX rocket

The Christmas Island community has been captivated by the rocket, which sheltered just off the coast.

A crew involved in the retrieval effort signed the wall of a local pub. (Supplied)

Local school students followed the Starship's movements, and social media feeds were flooded with images of the rocket, with a local dive company offering 'rocket trips'.

Bird enthusiasts turned rocket watchers on Christmas Island. (Supplied: Lisa Preston)

A local bar even named a cocktail Rocket Fuel in honour of the unexpected arrival, with crew members involved in the retrieval leaving a message on its wall.

Local tourism operator Lisa Preston has been hosting 30 birdwatchers for the island's annual Bird Week, who have been excited to witness the retrieval operation.

The arrival of the Space-X rocket has been a novelty for Christmas Island locals. (Supplied)

Ms Preston said it had been an amazing journey, and the Christmas Island community enjoyed being in the global spotlight.

"The decision being made to tow the rocket here when there's thousands of kilometres of coastline south of us, to be able to fulfil that role, to protect it whilst they did what they needed to do … it shows we've got alternate uses for positive things."

Expensive exercise

The journey of about 20,000 kilometres back to the Starbase rocket development facility in Texas is expected to take several weeks.

University of Sydney Professor of Marine Robotics Stefan Williams said the cost of the retrieval operation would add up quickly.

The retrieval of the Space-X craft from the water took many hours. (Supplied: Paul Hollier)

"We operate pretty regularly on research vessels which can cost $50,000 to $100,000 a day to operate, these are even bigger vessels," he said.

"There's a significant cost involved, both in rescue operations and also in the transport of the equipment from where it's been retrieved, in this case back to the home base in the US."

Rough weather hampered efforts to retrieve the rocket after splashdown. (SpaceX)

Professor Williams said semi-submersible vessels like the Forte were quite common, but using such a large ship was a heavy-duty operation.

"They're used extensively in the offshore industry in oil and gas and increasingly in offshore wind, anywhere you need large bits of equipment to be moved around," he said.

Starship 40's legacy

The 52-metre-long rocket is the first SpaceX upper stage spacecraft to survive a space flight intact and could provide a wealth of information for engineers.

SpaceX is hoping to launch, catch, and reuse its rockets going forward. (Supplied: SpaceX)

One of the goals for the space company is developing a rocket that can return safely to its launch site and be used again.

Astronomer Matt Woods says SpaceX's program is helping to make space exploration more affordable.

SpaceX's Starship 40 is heading back to the US after a controlled touchdown in the Indian Ocean on July 24. (Supplied: Svyatoslav Shanygin)

"Just off the back of the first stage of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy [rockets], it's dropped the price down on rockets dramatically," he said.

"It's amazing what you can do and how cheap it is for companies and universities to put the satellites up there and continue doing their study of the universe."

title: Teacher banned from teaching after sexual misconduct with former student
text:
A married high school teacher who had a sexual relationship with his former student has been banned from teaching for seven years.

The man taught the teenage girl for two and a half years between 2017 and 2019, before they allegedly began exchanging texts, and messages on the encrypted app Telegram.

It's alleged their relationship escalated, becoming physical and sexual in nature, after the student graduated.

He was 26-years-old when the misconduct started.

According to the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal judgement, the female student was in year 12, and 18-years-old, when she confided in her teacher about some mental health struggles one day after school.

The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal prohibited the man from teaching for seven years. (Supplied, Department of Justice)

It's alleged the pair then began communicating and meeting up, including outside the school library and on one occasion at a hotel while the teen was still enrolled at school.

On another date the teacher was allegedly witnessed by at least two people touching the students' legs under a table while the pair were playing board games at a camp.

In late 2019, the teen also allegedly gave her teacher a jar of lollies as a birthday gift, and on another occasion, handed him love letters which were later found by the man's wife.

"She found the handwritten letters in the glove box of the respondent's car," the judgement stated.

"The respondent took the letters from her, tore them up and put them in the recycling bin", then deleted photos of the letters from her phone without her knowledge or permission.

Some messages obtained by an investigator detailed a conversation about the teacher's former wife removing her wedding rings.

"Do you feel a little hurt? Like does it feel it feel more real. That yeah what's happening between you two is real?," the student asked her former teacher. "No, I don't feel hurt actually. Yeah it does make it feel more real, though, but I guess that was to be expected," he replied. "That's okay 🙂 just wish I could spend more time with you," he added.

Sexual relationship after graduation

According to the judgement, the misconduct escalated in 2020 after the student graduated high school, becoming an ongoing sexual relationship.

It included at least nine overnight stays, visits together to Springbrook National Park, a cinema, and a several week period where they sent over 1,400 texts.

The teacher was first suspended in April 2020, with the Queensland College of Teachers applying in 2024 to have him banned from teaching indefinitely, alleging misconduct on at least 15 occasions.

Among them were allegations the pair had kissed and engaged in other sexual acts while the student was still in school.

When questioned, the teacher and student both denied the allegations, with some unable to be proven as "the only evidence was second hand hearsay from a friend of the student".

Today the tribunal said an indefinite ban wouldn't be appropriate, instead prohibiting the teacher from reapplying for his registration and from teaching for seven years from when he was first suspended.

He will be eligible to teach again on November 30 this year.

In today's judgement the Queensland College of Teachers said it agreed with the Tribunal that "teachers are bestowed with a special trust by parents and the community to act in the best interest of students and to protect them from harm".

"And, with that trust, an expectation that it will not be breached," it said.

"Teachers exercise powers that have a significant impact on the lives of students.

"How teachers behave towards a student may influence that student for life.

"The standard applied to behaviour of a teacher both in their capacity as a teacher and behaviour which occurs outside of a school setting or with recent former students."

title: Nearly 900 patients contacted after colonoscopy audit
text:
Queensland Health is in the process of contacting almost 900 patients who had colonoscopy procedures at two southern Queensland hospitals after it was found that a doctor may not have met expected standards of care.

The health department says an audit raised questions about a private specialist's procedures at Goondiwindi and Warwick hospitals between 2023 and 2026.

The quality assurance audit identified 890 patients whose procedures may not have met the expected standard of care.

The specialist is no longer providing colonoscopy services within Darling Downs Health facilities, and a referral has been made to the Office of the Health Ombudsman.

Darling Downs Health acting chief executive Louise Van Every said there was no evidence that any patients had been harmed.

"Some of the procedures performed showed gaps in documentation and did not allow us to be sure the procedures met expected standards for colonoscopy care," she said.

Ms Van Every said the department was being proactive and contacting all impacted patients, despite 92 per cent being private patients.

"To make sure they are aware of the concerns identified and know where to go for appropriate follow-up care," she said.

title: Qld Fire Department to plead guilty to safety breach in fatal blaze
text:
The Queensland Fire Department will plead guilty to a safety breach in relation a fatal factory fire that took the life of beloved firefighter Izabella Nash in May 2023.

The 46-year-old known as Izzy, and fellow senior firefighter Lia Drew were each seriously injured while battling a warehouse blaze at Slacks Creek south of Brisbane.

Emergency crews managed to revive Izzy Nash at the scene, but she died the following day in hospital, while Lia Drew was treated for serious burns to her hands and arms.

Soon after, Workplace Health and Safety (OWHS) launched an investigation into the fatal incident, looking into whether rescue efforts were delayed or hampered on the day.

Workplace Health and Safety launched an investigation into the fatal incident, looking into whether rescue efforts were delayed or hampered on the day. (Supplied: QAS)

According to attending crews, firefighters struggled to reach the women due to severe conditions, heat and a single access point, later using a ladder to enter the factory via a window.

The investigation probed issues including the lack of a standard mayday call in emergency situations, whether there were thermal imaging cameras available which might have assisted crews, and whether staff were adequately trained in ladder rescues and breathing apparatuses.

Izabella Nash joined the Queensland Fire Department in 2014. (Supplied: QFES)

In 2025 the OWHS launched legal action against the Queensland Fire Department, stating it failed to comply with its health and safety duty by exposing an individual to a risk of death, serious injury or illness.

Today the department announced it would plead guilty to the breach, however reiterated it is not accused of causing Izzy Nash's death or Lia Drew's injuries.

"On 2 May 2023, the Queensland Fire Department (QFD) lost one of its own," it said in a statement.

"QFD has been working with the safety regulator and prosecutor since the incident and has today informed all relevant parties that QFD intends to plead guilty to the charge in the Work Health and Safety prosecution.

"The prosecution relates to alleged failures associated with fireground radio communications. However to be clear, it is not alleged that such failures caused the death of Izzy or the injury to Lia."

QFD Commissioner Steve Smith said the department has learnt from the "tragic incident". (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

Izzy Nash had been working as a firefighter for nearly a decade prior to her death, which QFD Commissioner Steve Smith described as a "profound tragedy".

"Her dedication, service and sacrifice will never be forgotten," he said in a statement.

"I want to reassure Queensland Fire and Rescue Firefighters and the Queensland community that the Queensland Fire Department has learnt from this tragic incident.

"Since the incident, the Queensland Fire Department has undertaken substantial work to strengthen structural firefighting safety."

A memorial was held for Ms Nash. (Supplied: QFES)

He said the department had since implemented 33 related recommendations, purchased new state-of-the-art intervention equipment, and provided staff with updated self-rescue and rapid intervention training.

"Our firefighters have played an active role in uplifting our capability," the commissioner said.

"Their discipline and dedication to their profession makes firefighting, which is an inherently dangerous job, safer.

"We are not finished; we will continue to adapt and evolve to meet the challenges of modern firefighting.

"My focus remains on supporting those affected by this incident, respecting the court process and doing everything reasonably practicable to keep firefighters and Queenslanders safe."

The Queensland Fire Department will be sentenced at a later date.

title: 'Not a pyromaniac': Teen who set off Perth Hills bushfire avoids jail
text:
A teenager who lit a homemade firecracker in bushland in the Perth Hills on New Year's Day, triggering an out-of-control fire that saw hundreds of people told to leave their homes, has avoided a prison sentence.

Luke Grguric, 19, threw the cracker, which he had made out of matches and cardboard, into the bush in Kalamunda shortly after watching the New Year's Eve fireworks on TV, the court heard. He proceeded to record the incident.

But instead of exploding as he had thought it would, the device set off a fire that quickly spread.

The bushfire reached emergency level in the Kalamunda- Maida Vale area before being downgraded. (Supplied)

The court earlier heard Grguric panicked as the fire took hold, and unsuccessfully tried to put it out by stomping on it, before alerting neighbours and emergency services.

Many properties in the bushfire-prone area had to be evacuated due to the fire, which required about 160 emergency personnel to tackle.

About 25 hectares of native vegetation was destroyed and 2,000 homes also lost power.

Firefighters were battling the blaze in the area. (Supplied: Kalamunda Volunteer Bush Fire Brigade)

Grguric had pleaded guilty to a charge of failing to ensure a fire or ignition source would not have caused a fire that could not be controlled.

In the District Court today he was given a suspended prison term of eight months.

'Foolish' and 'reckless'

Grguric's lawyer Alex Smith told the court his client was "not someone who's a pyromaniac" and that the fire was an isolated incident.

New Year's Day fire forces residents to flee homes A man has faced court after allegedly sparking an emergency-level bushfire in the Perth Hills that left thousands of people without power and threatened lives and homes.

"It was foolish, it was reckless but it was accidental," he said.

He told the court Grguric had been "experimenting with a firecracker" and had called emergency services himself.

The court also heard that Grguric felt "mortified" when he was taken into custody because he did not know what was happening with the fire.

Luke Grguric leaves court after being given a suspended prison term of eight months. (ABC News: David Weber)

During sentencing, Judge Martin Flynn described the incident as a "serious example of a breach of duty", but said everything Grguric did after the fire started was appropriate.

The 19-year-old did not speak to the media after leaving court.

title: Anita Perrottet asked to explain $660k in payments at corruption inquiry
text:
The wife of a key figure in a NSW corruption watchdog inquiry was paid more than $660,000 over two-and-a-half years, during which she worked an average of 16 hours a week, the probe has heard.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining allegations that prohibited political donations were funnelled through third parties to support a right-wing Liberal faction known as the NSW Reformers, to advance the interests of developer Jean Nassif, founder of Toplace.

Anita Perrottet is married to Charles Perrottet, a member of the Reformers and the brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.

The commission heard Ms Perrottet was paid a total of $660,999 by companies linked to lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood, Beckington and JPG Advisory.

Charles Perrottet is a member of a right-wing Liberal faction known as the NSW reformers. (Supplied: Facebook)

"That's an enormous amount of money to be paid for circumstances where you cannot produce a scrap of evidence in relation to work done," counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer put to Ms Perrottet.

Ms Perrottet said she believed she was paid what she was worth and Mr Greenwood saw her as a "huge value-add".

'An impossible situation'

The inquiry is also examining payments made to Ms Perrottet's company, Macquarie Consulting, and whether they were for genuine consulting work or used to disguise money allegedly intended for Charles Perrottet.

Earlier this week, the commission heard Ms Perrottet was paid $254,666 for three months of consulting work in 2022, despite saying her role largely involved verbal marketing and strategic advice and that she could recall little documentation of the work.

On Friday, Ms Perrottet was confronted with an email sent from her company account to lobbying firm Premier National, detailing issues with a Toplace development in Rosebery.

The email, signed by Ms Perrottet, said the owners were considering taking action against Mr Nassif over the development's lack of an occupancy certificate.

Dr Dwyer said the email appeared to show her "advocating" for Toplace and Mr Nassif, despite her evidence that neither had been a client.

Ms Perrottet said she could not recall sending the email.

Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif is expected to give evidence at the inquiry via video link. (Background Briefing: Cherine Yazbeck, file photo)

The commission previously heard Charles Perrottet had access to her account.

Dr Dwyer: I don't mean to embarrass you by that email. I'm suggesting you've been put in an impossible situation… That was not the email that you sent on behalf of Macquarie Consulting, was it? Ms Perrottet: I just don't recall it. It may have been me. Dr Dwyer: You're under oath. Do you seriously suggest that the commission would accept that you might have sent that detailed email in relation to Jean Nassif and Toplace? Ms Perrottet: It may have been. I do not recall.

'Monumental memory loss'

When Dr Dwyer suggested that Mr Perrottet wrote the email, Ms Perrottet said she could not remember and that it was possible he could have assisted her in writing it.

"You're not prepared to admit that [he wrote it] because you don't want to get your husband, Charles, in trouble for doing work for Jean Nassif and for Toplace," Dr Dwyer said.

Peggy Dwyer presses Ms Perrottet on her knowledge of the email. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

Ms Perrottet maintained she was telling the truth and trying to assist the commission.

"Toplace was not a client of mine. I never met Mr Nassif. I never had anything to do with him. I don't recall this email," Ms Perrottet said.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Dr Dwyer questioned how Ms Perrottet had experienced "such a monumental memory loss" in relation to the email.

While giving evidence on Friday, Ms Perrottet said she did not recall or remember, was not sure, or did not know on at least 200 occasions.

Ms Perrottet was also shown messages about a planned lunch at Mr Nassif's home, and photographs of her children there, but again she said she could not recall the event.

Dominic Perrottet, who referred the allegations to ICAC in 2022, is not accused of wrongdoing.

'The game is exposed'

Text messages between Charles and Ms Perrottet raised questions about her knowledge of Liberal factional dealings, including former NSW minister David Elliott’s political future.

Ms Perrottet previously told the ICAC she knew little about her husband's involvement in Liberal factional activities.

As Dominic Perrottet was becoming premier, messages show the couple discussing Mr Elliott’s prospects for a ministry.

In another exchange, Charles Perrottet wrote: “We execute the prick as soon as party room is over."

Dr Dwyer suggested the comment referred to Mr Elliott, but Ms Perrottet said she did not know what he meant.

Ms Perrottet was quizzed about text messages between her and husband Charles. (ABC News)



The commission was also shown emails and documents from Ms Perrottet's account relating to Greyhound Racing NSW, despite her evidence that her work for Mr Greenwood was largely verbal. The commission was also shown emails and documents from Ms Perrottet's account relating to Greyhound Racing NSW, despite her evidence that her work for Mr Greenwood was largely verbal.

Ms Perrottet said she could not remember creating the documents, prompting Dr Dwyer to say her evidence was “patently false.”

Dr Dwyer also questioned why the first recorded email between the pair came shortly after a parliamentary inquiry into alleged illegal donations was announced, suggesting it was sent to provide a “sham working arrangement” for Macquarie consulting.

"The game is exposed, isn’t it?," Dr Dwyer asked. "It is just completely ludicrous to maintain the position that … this was a genuine business." "It was a genuine business," Ms Perrottet responded.

'I wanted to appease' Nassif

Charles Perrottet entered the witness box on Friday afternoon, telling the inquiry he maintained contact with Mr Nassif and provided him with updates on Liberal Party affairs, also helping chase unpaid invoices owed to Beckington.

He said Mr Nassif frequently complained about his development projects and Mr Elliott.

"I wanted to appease him," Mr Perrottet told the commission.

"I humoured him at times because I had an ulterior motive to seek some information from him in regard to allegations that had been around."

Mr Perrottet gave evidence at the public inquiry for the first time on Friday. (ABC News)

The ICAC is examining whether donations linked to Mr Nassif were exchanged for political favours, including attempts to damage Mr Elliott's career.

Mr Perrottet said he would reassure Mr Nassif that his projects would be treated fairly, but that his actions inside the Liberal Party were different.

The commission previously heard allegations that money from Mr Nassif's Toplace was channelled through companies linked to Mr Greenwood, before being distributed to Mr Perrottet and others.

In her opening statement, Dr Dwyer said evidence would show Mr Perrottet, Mr Greenwood and lobbyist Chritsian Ellis anticipated receiving $2 million from Mr Nassif, split evenly between them.

She also alleged intercepted calls and messages indicated Mr Perrottet may have used his position in the Liberal Party to advance Mr Nassif's business interests.

title: McKeown says she has 'a lot of work to do' to reclaim world records
text:
Five-time Olympic champion Kaylee McKeown has opened up on the pain of watching her 50m world record get broken twice while she was sidelined with glandular fever and recovering from a broken wrist suffered this year.

"I've had some of my records taken from me, [and] I'd like to reclaim them," McKeown told ABC Sport.

"I think that [makes] your achievements very humbling with the fact that people can take them off you at any given moment.

"I can hold onto my medals, but world records are meant to be broken."

Teenager breaks Kaylee McKeown backstroke world record Italian teenager Sara Curtis has set a new world record in the women's 50m backstroke, beating the mark previously held by Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

McKeown's 50m backstroke record was broken across two different races at the European championships by Italian swimmer Sara Curtis, with the Australian arguing the result was "inevitable" after the introduction of three sprint events to the Los Angeles Olympics.

Breaststroke, butterfly and backstroke 50m races have been added to the 2028 calendar.

"You get pure sprinters coming in and to her credit she's done a phenomenal job, she's broken the world record by 0.3 or 0.4 seconds," McKeown said.

"I've got a lot of work to do.

"The fact that I'm able to chase somebody now and not be the chased is something I really relish."

This follows American Regan Smith breaking McKeown's 100m backstroke world mark in 2024.

McKeown is relishing the opportunity to chase down her competitors. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

The ultra-competitive McKeown's run of poor health forced her to miss the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacific Championships with glandular fever. She said watching the Dolphins' success from home was bittersweet.

"It's my favourite part of swimming, competing in events against the best in the world," she said.

"Unfortunately I missed that this year, but it has lit a fire in my belly just seeing the [Australian] swimmers do really well.

"Our Aussie swimmers had a really great Comm Games … they held up really well so I think we've got a really bright future heading into Brisbane 2032 and LA."

Rest 'the hardest thing' for competitor McKeown

Arguably the greatest backstroker of all time, McKeown said dealing with glandular fever had been a new challenge for someone used to being at peak fitness.

"That's the very challenging part, the feeling of not being able to do what you usually do," she said.

"The thing with glandular fever is you look fine from the outside but on the inside your body is just crying for more rest, more relaxation.

"That is the hardest thing for me, not only in the pool but outside the pool, so I've had to refrain from these activities [I'd normally do] to avoid getting chronic fatigue and going down that path."

McKeown says she has found it hard to watch from the sidelines, while she recovers. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

In contrast to her usual routine of nine training sessions per week, McKeown is currently limited to three as she builds slowly towards the 2027 World Aquatic Championships.

"It's been a really slow recovery," she said.

"It's always the biggest part of any campaign, the last year leading into the Olympics where you fine-tune everything. You see where your competitors are at and then you come back the year after for the Olympic Games.

"I had a really, really good year in 2023 leading into the Paris Olympics and I'm hoping for the same next year. Hopefully my health [holds up] and there's no broken wrists either."

And while she'll be 31 by the time Brisbane 2032 rolls around, McKeown has her sights firmly set on a home Olympics, drawing on Swedish returning mum Sarah Sjöström for inspiration.

McKeown has had to dial down her training regime to get on top of her health. (Supplied)

"It's different swimming 50m strokes, to 200 or 400 metre, so I'll definitely reassess after LA Olympic Games and hopefully get on track with my life outside the pool [then]," she said.

"[Sjöström] had a kid and she's back and on top of the world, so if I can do that I will definitely be at Brisbane 2032."

McKeown also continues to draw inspiration from her dad, who she lost in 2020, as she works towards the goal of representing her country in her home state.

"We're not granted to be on this Earth," she said.

"That's the way I really live my life: to take every day as you can."

4 Pines Park: The one thing Manly fans were looking forward did not happen on Friday evening. The Sea Eagles thumped a woeful St George Illawarra 44-10 to keep their slim finals hopes alive. Loading Manly simply need to beat the New Zealand Warriors next weekend and rely on South Sydney or the Cowboys losing both of their final two games to qualify. The Sea Eagles have the firepower and confidence to cause some headaches should they make it to September.

Advertisement

Who would want to stop Haumole Olakau’atu in full flight? Tom Trbojevic is two games back from a hamstring injury and also bound to strip fitter. And what about Clayton Faulolo, who bagged a try, set up another three and is proving arguably the best utility on the northern beaches? But the 13,957 supporters inside 4 Pines Park one last time this season, including members of the club’s 1996 premiership team, rose to their feet for the kick-off in the 74th minute when Nathan Brown was ready to launch himself off the back fence. Brown was playing his 200th NRL game and his last at home before finishing his career in the Super League next year. What Brown lacks in size he makes up for in heart, and quickly earned the reputation for his kick-off carries, not to mention the nickname “Back-fence Brown”.

Advertisement

The TV cameras captured Brown’s eyes light up when the Dragons kicked to his side of the field. The Italian international started to steam on to the ball, got excited, then realised the pass from Jamal Fogarty was never coming because he had dropped the ball. Brown let out a giant sigh, as did the supporters. Departing Manly forward Nathan Brown celebrated his 200th NRL game with a big win. NRL Photos “I felt for him because I saw him wind up about three or four times, he wanted to have one of those carries,” coach Kieran Foran said. “He’s been such a warrior, to get to 200 games and the way he’s had to do it – he’s stayed in the fight a long time – it was great to see him go out a winner [at home] tonight.” It was a shame, but it was never going to change the result.

Advertisement

As is the case every year, Manly are the one club teams above them probably do not want to meet in the finals. If they fall short, they will rue a few tight losses, including golden-point defeats to Canterbury and the Cowboys. It is still a success, considering they dropped their opening three games, sacked coach Anthony Seibold, then eventually appointed one of their favourite sons, Foran, to succeed him. Things will become a lot clearer about the September hopes in the next few days. The future looks bright, regardless, when you think of a player like Faulolo, as well as Onitoni Large, who made his debut with 20 minutes remaining, and was given a warm embrace by Trbojevic as he took the field.

Advertisement

Large is just 19, was in the Wests Tigers system before signing a three-year deal with Manly, and was just as handy at rugby. Foran is confident he has a big future: “The thing I love about Onitoni [during] the last six weeks is the growth we’ve seen in his game; we felt like he was so ready if he was called upon. He’s going to be a special player. He’s young, raw, but he works hard on his game.” Josh Feledy keeps the points coming for the Sea Eagles on Friday night. Getty Images The Sea Eagles were given a standing ovation when they led 26-0 at the break against a Dragons side that completed only 10 of their 15 sets. Things did not improve for the men wearing red and white in the second half. The Dragons will finish with the wooden spoon. At least they have recruited well and have plenty to get excited about in 2027. Still, they will want to finish on a high next week on home soil, and send out the likes of the departing Damien Cook on a high.

title: From the hand of Dan: A secret tax, a handwritten note, and a hard lesson for Ben Carroll
text:
Ben Carroll has kept a handwritten note from Daniel Andrews as a reminder of how not to govern.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ben Carroll was sitting in his Bali hotel room on a family holiday when he received a call from a journalist seeking confirmation on a big story – that the Melbourne Airport Rail Link, a major infrastructure project close to Carroll’s heart, had been shelved. Carroll was adamant the Herald Sun reporter had gotten the wrong end of the stick. “You’re completely wrong,” he told him. “I’m the public transport minister. It goes through my electorate. We took this to the 2022 election. I would know about it.” The following day, the paper duly splashed with the news that the project had been mothballed, ostensibly due to concerns about the state’s rising debt. Carroll was furious. He was later informed, through a three-way telephone conversation with then treasurer Tim Pallas and deputy premier Jacinta Allan, that the decision had indeed been made, in secret and without his knowledge, by the Expenditure Review Committee, a meeting of four senior ministers chaired by Daniel Andrews. Then-premier Jacinta Allan with Ben Carroll in May. Eddie Jim It was a Saturday morning in April 2023, in the final months of the Andrews government. Two days later, Carroll was back at work in his usual spot around the cabinet table and still steaming. Andrews, sensing the heat rising from his minister, wrote a message on a sticky note and passed it to Carroll. “We’ve got the sequence (at last) right on MARL,” it read.

Advertisement

More than three years later, Carroll still has the note pinned above his desk as a reminder of how not to govern. The story is well known among the new premier’s trusted circle, two of whom relayed it to The Age, both for what it says about the secretive, highly centralised way in which Andrews ran the state, and Carroll’s determination to do things differently if he ever got the chance. It also helps explain why Carroll was genuinely outraged when he this week discovered, through the meticulous reporting of the Victorian Auditor General’s Office, the full, malodorous history of the Rail Improvement Charge (RIC), a hidden levy on public transport users that has sat on the state’s books – or rather, off book – since the start of last year. Related Article Suburban Rail Loop How Allan, ministers decided to hide public transport levy in secret talks The auditor-general’s report was tabled in parliament on Wednesday, when Carroll was in Sydney for a meeting of national cabinet. He was briefed on its contents but reserved judgement until he read the full report. That happened the next morning when he rose early, printed off its 170 pages at home and scoured it cover to cover. A short time later, he drove into parliament and announced that he was scrapping the RIC and apologised for the entire episode. “There was no transparency on the creation and implementation of this charge,” he said. The RIC, a 1 per cent levy on top of all public transport fares conceived as a new revenue source to finance the Suburban Rail Loop, came into force on January 1 last year and was forecast to funnel $8 billion into government coffers over the next 36 years.

Advertisement

Its sudden death, so shortly after the belated news of its birth, punches a hole in the government’s capacity to service its debt splurge on major infrastructure and raises further doubts about the financial viability of the state’s largest transport construction project, the SRL. The auditor-general’s report – an audit to determine whether the SRL East, the first stage of the 90-kilometre Suburban Rail Loop, is progressing within the government’s stated time frame and budget – does more than trace the history of a curious little tax. Through its forensic account, and The Age’s subsequent conversations with ministers, MPs and bureaucrats who were not authorised to speak publicly, it opens a window on a much deeper problem – the culture of secrecy and control that infected the Andrews and Allan governments. The question it raises for voters in the lead up to the state election is whether they believe that Carroll and his November running mate, Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams, are genuinely committed to greater transparency in government or whether, as long-serving members of the previous administrations, they were part of the problem. Carroll and Gabrielle Williams took charge of the state government last month. Jason South Carroll and Williams have known of the rail charge, though not its full history, since 2024. “There are multiple occasions where the RIC was discussed involving both of them,” one former minister said. “At what point does it stop being incompetence and start to be willful blindness?” Auditor-General Andrew Greaves’s report reveals the charge was conceived five years ago by Pallas and Andrews, in the depths of the COVID crisis, to prop up the investment and business case for the SRL. It was kept secret from all but a small club of senior ministers and departmental officials.

Advertisement

The rail loop business case was published in August 2021, the same month which, according to Greaves, the government first approved a plan to use 60 per cent of RIC revenue – an estimated $4.8 billion between 2025 and 2062 – to repay borrowings for the SRL. More accurately, this is when the plan was approved by the Expenditure Review Committee chaired by Andrews. The other members of the committee were treasurer Pallas, the then minister for the SRL Jacinta Allan and James Merlino, the deputy premier who would go on to chair the Suburban Rail Loop Authority. The decision never went to full cabinet. This is consistent with how Andrews governed. His approach, one borrowed by British Labour luminary Tony Blair, was to elevate a series of subcommittees, all of which he chaired, into discreet, executive forums that operated at arms’ length from cabinet. Sometimes decisions made by subcommittees were reported back to the cabinet, but often they weren’t. Ministers would sometimes be invited to present to subcommittees on matter relating to their portfolio responsibilities, but not always. One former departmental official who sat in on the meetings of one subcommittee said that once a decision was taken, the next order of business would be working out how to tell the minister responsible for overseeing it. Carroll was not alone in learning about a big decision impacting his portfolio on the front page of a newspaper. Decisions of the Andrews government were often not considered by his full cabinet. Jason South

Advertisement

In August 2021, when Andrews and Pallas were nutting out the Rail Improvement Charge, Carroll was the minister for public transport but none the wiser that a new tax on fares was being developed. “I was not part of the creation,” he said this week. Other government ministers told The Age they first heard of the charge when the auditor-general’s report splashed like a brick into the Spring Street pond. “The scales fell from my eyes today,” one current minister said after the report was tabled. Another explained: “You’ve got to remember there was a practice in that previous term of government of putting decisions through the smallest possible collectives of ministers. That was a practice that was started by Daniel and it was continued by Jacinta. What it led to was a complete lack of visibility of policy by the broader cabinet.” The Suburban Rail Loop, a project conceived in secret by private consultants with the knowledge of some of the government’s most senior transport officials, was a product of this culture. The Suburban Rail Loop Authority, the statutory authority created in 2019 to oversee the project, is renowned for the distance it keeps between itself and government departments that overlap with its work. Related Article Public service Thrown in a loop: How Daniel Andrews’ biggest project was cooked up behind closed doors Greaves identifies this problem in his report. He refers to a previously unpublished government review of the authority, which in 2024 raised concerns about “issues with trust, co-operation, information flows and role clarify between the SRLA and central agencies.” Put simply, people on different sides of the SRL wall did not talk to each other. One example of this was a decision taken by the SRLA board to order a pause in negotiations with construction firms over cost over-runs. The board didn’t bother to seek approval from the government for this decision on the management of the state’s largest infrastructure project. A recurring symptom of an unaccountable culture is the frustration expressed by ministerial and departmental staff who tried to get information out of the authority. Two days before the auditor-general’s report was tabled, Carroll announced his intention to wind up the SRLA and fold its functions into another government agency.

title: There’s one key reason female GPs like me are quitting
text:
Advertisement

NationalHealthcare Opinion There’s one key reason female GPs like me are quitting Elly Goodsall Doctor August 28, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 28, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal government has announced that 84.1 per cent of visits to general practitioners are now bulk billed, and has called that progress. The figure counts the doctors who’ve stayed in the profession. After 13 years, I am not one of them. About four years ago, a patient walked into my consulting room struggling – she told me that much. What she could not yet tell me was that she had a specific plan to end her life, and the means to carry it out. She came back recently to tell me that because of the time and kindness of that first appointment, her children have a mother today. Dr Elly Goodsall, who is quitting as a GP after 13 years in practice, citing the pressures on the “underclass” of female doctors. I have thought about that a great deal. Not with pride, but with the weight of it. She was not describing anything exceptional that I did. She was describing what becomes possible when a GP makes enough time to sit with a person. To notice. To make someone feel that they are worth an hour of another human being’s unhurried attention. That is not a luxury. That is general practice. I am not leaving because I want to. It is the vigilance of never being allowed to miss anything. It is the patient distress carried home. It is the unpaid hours that continue after the last patient has gone. And it is all of that inside a system whose government will not acknowledge, in anything but words, what a good GP is worth. I have been filling the gap between the care I refuse to compromise on and the support I receive to provide it – with my own time, my own earnings, and emotional reserves my children also deserved. I am done.

Advertisement

Female GPs carry a more complex and less remunerated caseload than our male colleagues. In the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners’ 2024 Health of the Nation survey, nearly eight in 10 female GPs named psychological issues among their three most common patient presentations, compared with just over six in 10 male GPs. Women’s health appeared in the top three for 52 per cent of female GPs and 3 per cent of male GPs. Male GPs reported more musculoskeletal, respiratory, circulatory and skin presentations. Complexity takes longer, and it shows: female GPs spend on average three minutes more with every patient. We are also more likely to bulk-bill those who cannot afford to pay, and to run over time because a person needed more than 15 minutes. Related Article Medicare Free GP visits on the rise as 1400 clinics ditch out-of-pocket fees Medicare pays per consultation, not per minute. An analysis by Ochre Health of 511 GPs across its practices found the women billed about $24 an hour less than the men – a gap driven almost entirely by the number of appointments fitted into an hour, not by what women charged. We are not paid less for the same work. We are paid less for more complex work that unavoidably requires more time. The government is telling you that GPs refusing to bulk-bill are the problem. We are not. The problem is an unwillingness to invest meaningfully in general practice, and a determination to disguise that. The “triple bulk-billing incentive” tripled not the bulk-billed rate but a small incentive payment – a pebble thrown into a cavern, with a press release claiming that the cavern was filled and that GPs simply needed to step up. This is not ignorance. Asked at the National Press Club in April whether longer consultations should attract a higher rebate, the minister accepted that female GPs do longer consultations, more mental health work and more complex multi-condition care – but also said he had reached that view on anecdotal evidence, without necessarily seeing the hard data.

Advertisement

I would rather leave than practise Band-Aid medicine. I would earn considerably more doing exactly that – shorter appointments, higher throughput, less emotional investment. The financial logic is obvious. I have never been able to make myself do it. It takes time to build the trust that lets someone finally tell you the thing they have never told anyone. Patients know when you care. The trust inside that relationship is the thing that heals. Related Article Opinion

Gender pay gap We're paid less to do so much more: one female doctor speaks out I am not alone. A study published late last year in the Australian Health Review by Professor Louise Stone, Professor Karen Price and colleagues surveyed 770 female GPs who had left or drastically reduced their clinical hours. They described themselves as an underclass, doing the profession’s invisible emotional labour for a fraction of the remuneration, and named government narratives around bulk-billing as a key driver of their exit. The authors called what these women experienced “malignant disregard”. I recognise every word. Australia faces a projected shortfall of more than 11,000 full-time-equivalent GPs by 2032. Women now make up nearly half the workforce, and we have been given a shorter expiry date. A longitudinal study of more than 4000 Australian GPs found the median age at which women left clinical practice was 47; for men, most exits came after 67. Here is what should trouble you: women were not planning to go. Mothers of young children reported lower intentions to leave than their colleagues – and left at higher rates anyway. We do not leave because we have stopped caring. We leave because we have been caring, at extraordinary personal cost, in a system that has decided not to look.

Advertisement

My patient’s children have a mother today because of a long appointment with a GP who had time to notice. That is what is being lost. Not a statistic, not a workforce number, but a particular quality of attention that keeps people out of emergency departments and out of crisis. Related Article Exclusive

Investigation Jeanne-Marie survived ‘mother of all surgeries’, but bias nearly broke her. How to fix medical misogyny I leave with profound gratitude for every patient who trusted me with their most difficult moments. They have been the privilege of my professional life. But a system that mistakes the sound of a pebble for the work of repair is not one I can afford to wait for any longer. Across Australia, female GPs are saying this out loud. I am one of them, and I will not be the last. Dr Elly Goodsall is leaving general practice after working as a GP in Newcastle since 2013. title: From Heartbreak Hill to hometown hero: Can a local star win the Sydney Marathon?
text:
Advertisement

SportAthleticsSydney Marathon From Heartbreak Hill to hometown hero: Can a local star win the Sydney Marathon? Iain Payten August 28, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Without a hint of heartbreak, Andy Buchanan recently won the City2Surf in a canter – and the experience provided two insights about his chances in the upcoming Sydney Marathon. Buchanan, who was the Australian marathon record holder until last month, is the leading local contender in the 42.195km slog on Sunday morning, which begins in North Sydney before winding through the city and out to Kingsford, then back to the Opera House. Andy Buchanan, the leading Australian male entrant in the Sydney Marathon, posing under the Harbour Bridge. Sam Mooy It is a notoriously rolling course with plenty of elevation, but Buchanan is comfortable with climbing, given his training base in Bendigo. Furthermore, the 35-year-old recently finished his preparation for the Sydney Marathon by cruising to a win over the shorter, but similarly hilly, 14km City2Surf course. “I’m really confident, the City to Surf felt quite easy and comfortable, which was a great sign,” Buchanan said. “I ran the Gold Coast Half [in July] poorly and knew I could do better, so I wanted another race to build confidence.

Advertisement

“I spoke to my coach about doing another race and he floated City to Surf. We were nervous about the hills beating my legs up three weeks out from a marathon, but the week before, I decided I really wanted to do it. So I entered that week. “I grew up in Bendigo and run hills every single day, so I’m used to it. I’m confident with hills; they don’t scare me.” Buchanan crossed the line at Bondi Beach in a time of 40 minutes, 27 seconds. It was still 23s adrift of the record set by Steve Moneghetti in 1991, who was then at the peak of his powers. The distance legend had won his first marathon in Berlin a year earlier, and remains one of only three Australians to win a Major, along with Robert DeCastella (Boston, 1986) and Lisa Ondieki, who won in New York in 1992.

Advertisement

Buchanan would love to join those Aussie icons on an elite list, but his time at the finishing gate in Bondi was a good reminder of the form required. “Moneghetti was an absolute phenomenon. I tried to beat his record a few weeks ago at City to Surf and didn’t get near it,” Buchanan said. “[Winning a major] definitely motivates me, but the running world has changed a lot from when ‘Monner’ was running. Steve Moneghetti winning the 1991 City to Surf in 40:03, which is still the record. Ben Rushton/Fairfax Media “What I love about running is that it’s so accessible—literally every country in the world runs and has access to it. Think about how many countries have a 50-metreswimming pool; probably half the world. “Whereas with running, everyone runs. The game has changed over the last five or six years. It would be an absolute fairytale to win a major, especially here in my home country, but you have to be realistic when you’re up against guys running 2:01, 2:02, or 2:03. It’s a bit different.”

Advertisement

Much has changed indeed. The marathon world record stood at 2:06:50 until 1998, but in the decades since, 448 men have officially run under that time, and the world record has been slashed by almost seven minutes. African runners now dominate distance running, with almost 90 per cent of those 448 born in Africa. Buchanan is one of two Australians in the remaining 10 per cent, with a PB of 2:06.22 set in Valencia in 2024. His time broke the national record, but it was lowered last month – just – by Haftu Strintzos, who ran a 2:06.20 on the Gold Coast. DeCastella (2:08.18 in 1981) and Moneghetti (2:08.16 in 1990) sit slightly behind in eligible PBs, but there were no supershoes in that era. Over the last decade, high-tech, energy-saving footwear has helped slash average times of elite runners by several minutes. Buchanan, a chilled-out former teacher and shoe-shop owner, has said losing his record to Strintzos felt like getting hit by “1000 cement trucks” but he is motivated to regain it. That probably won’t happen in Sydney, where fast times are tough to achieve. Wins, too, given there are 18 athletes in the Sydney field with PBs under 2:06.

Advertisement

But the race within a race in Sydney is to be the first Australian male and female finisher. The Sydney Marathon provides $30,000 prizemoney for the two Australian winners, and $20,000 and $10,000 for minor placings. It is a huge sum for cash-strapped Australian runners. “Running is a tough sport, and we don’t get the financial support that a lot of other sports get,” Buchanan said. “It’s great that the Sydney Marathon is investing back into the Australian field. For $30,000, I’m already getting into Tim [Vincent] and Liam’s [Boudin] heads, reminding them how hilly it is compared to flat Brisbane. It’s definitely a race within a race.” In the women’s field, the leading Australian contenders are Olympians Ellie Pashley, Caitlin Scott and Milly Clark.

Advertisement

Related Article Sydney Marathon Marathon, not a sprint: Why Sydney’s beast of a course rewards power over pace Pashley, a mum of two, is hitting good form after winning the Ballarat Marathon in April, and Scott showed her huge potential by winning the Melbourne marathon on debut in 2025. Clark is also a past winner of the Melbourne marathon. “I’m really excited, to be honest. I think time off from the sport really grows your hunger to get back into it,” Pashley said. “Watching last year, seeing the course, seeing the race among the Australian women, I was really pumped to try and get a spot in the race this year.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was on a pilgrimage on the China-Nepal border when the catastrophic flash flooding hit.

Her husband Kailash Mansowar, who has not heard from her since, has travelled to the region from Sydney to find her, guided only by her iPhone's last location.

"I am here in Nepal now (since) yesterday and working with local authorities to find further information," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) on Friday.

Like many missing Australians, Adhikari was undertaking a group tour, in her case with the Isha Foundation.

She left Kathmandu on 14 August after flying from Sydney to trek to a sacred site near Tibet's Mount Kailash.

"Even the smallest piece of information could help bring her home," a widely shared post on social media announcing her disappearance reads.

A separate group of 15 Australians, including two boys aged 11 and 14, were travelling with US-based tourism operator Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company.

Sydney doctor Manoj Dharmaratnam, who was invited to join the sacred pilgrimage but chose not to go, prescribed several of his friends altitude medication and conducted injury assessments before they left Australia.

"One of them had an injury and I did tell her, maybe you're not fit to go on this trek," Dr Dharmaratnam told AAP.

"She actually called up and cancelled her trip ... but then she said I've bought the ticket, so I might as well go."

The Himalayan Glacier group included a well-respected Sydney couple with two sons in their 20s, both studying medicine in NSW, he said.

At least four Australians were travelling separately to tour groups, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Friday.

Wong said the federal government would send additional personnel to the region and unveiled a $5 million assistance package and humanitarian support.

An initial team of three humanitarian response specialists will be sent to help 20 staff already on the ground in Nepal.

But Chinese and Nepalese authorities say local rescue efforts could be complicated by further flooding, caused by a build-up of debris.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Thursday warned a lake was forming above the Rasuwagadhi border.

By Friday it had begun to overflow.

The Lhendi River had been obstructed about 18 kilometres above the border, posing a risk to residents in areas below, it said in a statement on social media.

The threat of a second flood caused by a blockage upstream led to evacuation orders at Jilong Port on the Nepal-China border, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

Rocks, boulders and debris lodged in the valley, as well as lakes forming along the plateau, could cause further flooding, geoscientist Jakob Steiner told AAP.

"Unfortunately it's not over ... this material is only going to lie there. We cannot move it away," Steiner, a fellow at the Asian Mountain Alliance, said.

"Every time a new flood comes, it's going to move this, and this is just going to increase future flood events in terms of impact."

title: How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods
text:
IN BRIEF Donations will help provide emergency shelter, food, clean water, hygiene supplies and medical care.

Australians can donate through the Emergency Action Alliance's Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal or by calling 1300 939 000.

Entire communities have been devastated by severe flooding and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border, with homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure destroyed.

Search and rescue operations remain underway, while thousands of people are in urgent need of shelter, food, clean drinking water and medical assistance.

In response, 14 Australian charities have joined forces to launch a national appeal.

Emergency Action Alliance

The Emergency Action Alliance (EAA) has launched the Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal, bringing together a variety of charities to support communities affected by the disaster.

The charities involved are continuing to assess the scale of the disaster and humanitarian needs in affected communities.

The EAA says its members are working to determine where support is most urgently needed as search and rescue operations continue.

The appeal has been endorsed by the Australian Council for International Development (ACFID), the peak body for Australian non-government organisations involved in humanitarian action and international development.

The ABC is also supporting the appeal through its ABC Gives initiative.

ACFID CEO Matthew Maury said coordinated action was critical as humanitarian needs continued to emerge.

Australia will also deploy three humanitarian specialists to Nepal within 48 hours to help assess needs and support the emergency response.

The specialists are being deployed through the Australia Assists program and have expertise in humanitarian assessment, logistics, communications and planning.

A crisis response team member and a regional consular officer are already on the ground in Kathmandu, alongside staff at the Australian embassy.

"With roads and bridges destroyed, many communities remain isolated and difficult to reach, underscoring the need for rapid humanitarian assistance," she said.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is working with Nepali authorities, tour operators and others to verify their welfare and contact their families.

title: Questions were mounting at the border. Then they found a tunnel
text:
In brief A migrant tunnel between Belarus and Latvia has deepened a longstanding rift.

The tunnel's discovery has widened an already deep rift between the two countries.

Latvia's border guard has accused Belarusian authorities of partial responsibility for a recently discovered migrant tunnel beneath a border fence between the two nations.

The tunnel was uncovered by Latvian authorities in early August. Latvia faces an increasing number of migrants trying to cross the border from Belarus, further straining relations between the two countries.

Latvia shares a 173km border with Belarus. Latvia is a member of the European Union. Belarus, an independent nation with an authoritarian government, is not.

At the time of the tunnel's discovery, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said criminal networks were facilitating migration from Belarus into Latvia, bringing migrants into Europe's borderless Schengen area, but that the migrants' final destination was elsewhere on the continent.

"They migrate to where it's easier (to enter the EU). So we must not be the easiest place," Kulbergs told the press conference.

He pledged to target networks transporting the migrants from the border to their destinations, as well as any support points for migrants in Latvia, as part of what he called "Operation Werewolf".

"If everything goes according to plan, we are confident that we will already deal a serious enough blow to the system," Kulbergs said. "I want to tell the organisers: everything will be put to an end."

Latvia's government said in a statement it would cooperate with neighbours Estonia, Lithuania, Poland and others to stop the flow of migrants.

Latvia, along with Lithuania and Poland, has frequently accused Belarus' authoritarian government of smuggling migrants from crisis-impacted regions close to the EU's far borders.

The plot thickens

Having now discovered a second tunnel at another point along the border fence, Latvia is pointing fingers at the Belarusian border guard.

"It is simply impossible to build such a tunnel without the Belarusian border guards being aware of it," Guntis Pujats, head of the agency, told Latvian radio on Thursday.

Pujats went on to give more information about the original tunnel, saying that the entrance on the Belarusian side of the border was found around 10m from the border line and had been hidden among trees and bushes. The tunnel itself was reported to be 80cm wide and to run for roughly 30m.

Some 28 cubic metres of earth had been removed to construct the tunnel. Support structures had been erected within the tunnel to keep it from collapsing, and a plywood cover had been fitted to the entrance.

"The construction work was quite extensive. So the relevant authorities were undoubtedly aware of it," he said.

Pujats claimed that 12 underground tunnels have been found across Lithuania, along with the two found in Latvia to date.

The Belarusian government has not publicly commented on the existence of the tunnels.

title: France's cheese makers are confronting a problem tradition alone can't solve
text:
In brief A summer of record-breaking heatwaves and drought has taken a toll on France.

The unusually hot and dry conditions have started to affect France's beloved and protected cheesemakers.

Widespread drought and record-breaking heatwaves have forced France to relax some of its famously strict rules on cheese production, with authorities announcing special measures for abondance, beaufort and comte.

France's vast array of local cheeses are a source of national pride, and authorities go to great lengths to protect traditional production methods and ensure authenticity.

To earn a coveted "appellation d'origine protegee" (Protected Designation of Origin) label — and the right to give their cheese a particular protected name — producers must follow rigid rules on where their animals graze and what they eat.

But the summer's drought, which affected 95 per cent of mainland France in July, has left normally rich pastures dry and bare.

In response, the government said this week that producers of abondance, beaufort and comte, hard cheeses made from the raw milk of cows grazing in the Alps and Jura mountains, can supplement the animals' diet with more fodder and grain brought in from elsewhere.

Growth on permanent grasslands as of 10 August is a third less than the 1989-2018 average, according to the agriculture ministry's statistical service.

The fodder situation is "highly degraded" in almost all regions, the ministry said earlier this month.

The National Institute of Origin and Quality (INAO), the government agency that administers and enforces rules of origin, says it will also grant temporary relief for several other cheeses including reblochon, cantal, bleu d'Auvergne, and fourme d'Ambert.

In France, farmers are bracing for their smallest corn crop since 1980, and winegrowers are reporting some of the earliest harvests on record.

title: Nepal army races to save 100 people trapped in tunnel as flood death toll rises to 469
text:

title: This Australian crisis is entering a 'confronting' new phase
text:
IN BRIEF More than 2,500 Australians died from drug-induced overdose in 2024, the highest on record.

Older Australians accounted for almost half of reported deaths.

This article contains references to substance abuse and suicide.

Drug-induced deaths have hit a record high, with older Australians accounting for more than half of the fatalities.

Australia's Annual Overdose Report, released by the Penington Institute, documented 2,596 drug-induced deaths in 2024, with 80.5 per cent being from unintentional overdose.

Since 2008, more Australians have died from drug-induced deaths than road fatalities — with an average of 31 years lost per death.

"The data is quite confronting," Jake Dizard, director of research at the Penington Institute, told SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The report found that the median age of people dying from drug overdose is increasing.

For the first time, those aged between 50 and 59 accounted for almost half of all unintentional overdose deaths.

Dizard said it could be attributed to "an ageing large cohort of people who started using drugs in the 1990s and early 2000s".

"As that cohort has got older, they have become more vulnerable to drug-induced death because of the length of time that they have been using drugs and the accumulating sort of comorbidities," he said.

The report also noted that of the 428 drug-induced suicides, 39 per cent were people aged 60 and over.

Australian Alcohol and Other Drugs Council CEO Melanie Walker said the report confirms that overdose is not a "young people problem".

"Overdose is something that affects the whole community," she told SBS News.

"It affects young people. It also affects older people. Overdose can be from illicit drug use, or it can be from prescription drug use."

The report also found that men accounted for 72.7 per cent of unintentional drug-induced deaths, people living in regional and rural areas had higher rates of death than those living in capital cities, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people experienced higher rates of overdose.

In 2024, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people experienced an overdose rate of 29.3 per 100,000 compared to 6.6 per 100,000 for non-Indigenous people.

Opioids were responsible for 42 per cent of all drug-induced deaths in 2024, with heroin-related deaths rising from 101 deaths in 2001 to 488 deaths in 2024.

Amphetamines were involved in 772 deaths, a record high for the drug, and cocaine was involved in 141 deaths. Benzodiazepines, alcohol and antidepressants also contributed to drug-induced deaths.

Dizard said that the use of prescription opioids, such as oxycodone, has declined since 2021 — a trend seen across "a number of categories of prescription drugs".

Cocaine was the only recorded drug that saw a decrease in the median age of people dying from overdose.

Two-thirds of Australians turned away from services

The majority of drug-induced deaths in Australia are preventable, Dizard said.

The report listed a range of recommendations to reduce the number of deaths, including increased access to the medicine naloxone.

"It's an opioid overdose reversal drug, which is very safe and can be administered by anybody," Dizard said.

"It's important not just for people who habitually or routinely use opioids, but also people who might be using other drugs, including cocaine, that might be contaminated with some sort of opioid."

Dizard noted the importance of community education on how to identify signs of overdose and respond — and greater investment in services, specifically opioid pharmacotherapy.

While stigma hinders people's ability to seek support for drug and alcohol addiction, Dizard said a major issue is a lack of funding for services.

He said law enforcement is heavily funded, and a "more balanced approach to drug policy" is needed.

"Funding has been incredibly unbalanced throughout the last several decades of Australian drug policy."

Australia's National Drug Strategy has three pillars: supply reduction, which includes law enforcement; demand reduction, which refers to treatment; and harm reduction, including preventative measures such as drug checks.

"The supply reduction pillar has traditionally had double the funding of treatment," Walker said.

She said that more than two-thirds of people seeking help for drug and alcohol use have been turned away from services because of funding insufficiency.

Walker said there's currently no forum for governments, both federal and state and territory, to come together and "talk about the implementation of the national drug strategy and do coordinated planning".

"For at least the last 10 years, half a million Australians have been missing out on getting to alcohol and other drug treatment because there's simply no place for them," she said.

"It's really obvious what the problem is in terms of why overdose deaths are rising, and until we come to terms with that and get proper resources — I can't see that changing."

SBS News has contacted the Department of Health for comment.

title: 'Creative thinking is born of loneliness': Artist Yayoi Kusama dies at 97
text:
In brief Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama died in hospital in Tokyo earlier this month.

The artist was famous for her enigmatic polka dot designs.

The dotty pumpkins and kaleidoscope rooms of Yayoi Kusama, who has died aged 97, were as vibrant as the artist herself, but her exuberant work was the expression of a long battle with mental illness.

Once a fixture of the 1960s pop and minimalist scenes in New York, Japan's "polka dot queen" found huge commercial success in her later decades.

Her larger-than-life paintings, sculptures and installations — inspired by vivid hallucinations — sold for millions of dollars and packed out top galleries.

Kusama, instantly recognisable in her bright red wig and bold spotted outfits, worked well into old age from the psychiatric hospital in Tokyo where she lived voluntarily for the second half of her life.

But she also struggled with her feelings for her home country, which she left for decades and once described as "full of disdain for women".
