Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Born in 1929, the youngest daughter of a wealthy but troubled family, Kusama started producing her signature dot and net patterns at the age of 10.

"My mother had regrets about my birth, and I was driven to the edge psychologically," she wrote in her autobiography, A Personal History of Polka Dots.

"One day, after seeing a tablecloth with a red flower pattern on a desk, I saw the same red flower pattern all over the ceiling, windows and pillars. It filled the room, and covered my body."

Art provided a release for the young Kusama, whose father, a seedling merchant, was unfaithful to her mother.

"When I was sad or lonely, everything would be cured when I drew pictures," she said.

In the book, Kusama explained her concept of "self-obliteration" — a recurrent theme throughout her career.

"I put dots all over my body and make all the surroundings dot patterns. By creating the same thing over and over, my own existence is buried in the art."

60s 'happenings'

Kusama studied Japanese painting in Kyoto, against her parents' wishes, and held her first solo exhibition in 1952 in her hometown of Matsumoto in central Japan.

At the show, she met a psychiatrist who advised her to go and work abroad — an idea that appealed to her.

"Japan was so small, vulgar, feudalistic and full of disdain for women," said the artist.

"I was born and raised in Japan, but I'm not influenced by Japanese culture and tradition."

The decisive push to pack her bags came when she wrote to modernist painter Georgia O'Keeffe, who encouraged Kusama to seek international recognition in the United States.

Yayoi Kusama's installation "Infinity Mirrored Room— The Hope of the Polka Dots Buried in Infinity Will Eternally Cover the Universe". Source: AFP / Ina Fassbender

Kusama moved to Seattle in 1957 and then to New York, where she struggled to find her place as an Asian artist in the city's largely white, male-dominated creative scene.

"I was at the lowest point of poverty. One time, I couldn't eat for three days because I had no money," she once told Japan's Asahi Shimbun newspaper.

"I even ate the breadcrumbs left by the pigeons."

But she persevered and, during her 16 years in New York, became a prominent figure in the avant-garde world.

At the height of the 1960s sexual liberation movement, she would stage "happenings", where people stripped naked on Wall Street or in Central Park and had their bodies painted with polka dots.

In 2024, Yayoi Kusama's iconic dots wrapped 60 plane trees in Melbourne. Source: AFP / William West

She also launched a fashion line, established a "Church of Self-Obliteration" and styled herself the "High Priestess of Polka Dots" to officiate at a gay wedding.

Global fame

By the time she returned to Japan in 1973, Kusama was burned out, and checked herself into a psychiatric ward where she lived for the rest of her life.

And it was not until the 1990s that her vivid patterns, bold floral shapes and shiny steel orbs hit the mainstream, later providing the backdrop to countless selfies.

Pumpkins are her most famous motif, featuring heavily in her paintings and giant sculptures.

The artist called them her "life partners", saying she had first grown to love their "generous, unpretentious looks" as a child.

Kusama was named the world's most popular artist in 2014 by The Art Newspaper.

She was also one of the most expensive, with one of her "infinity net" paintings fetching nearly US$8 million ($11 million) at a 2019 auction.

But fame and fortune did not affect her remarkable originality, which she once attributed to the "serenity of the soul" that comes from spending time alone.

"Creative thinking is born of loneliness ... because I stood before the art all alone, I was able to forge my own path," Kusama said.

She published several novels in her later years, while her exhibitions continued to draw huge crowds.

"My wish after my death is that the eternally bright future, the beauty of human love and my soul will be passed on," Kusama told reporters in 2017.

"Please love my artwork, even after I die."

Kusama died on 14 August in Tokyo.

title: Albanese reveals humanitarian visa intake won't be cut, amid migration reform questions
text:
in brief Reporting had suggested the government was considering cuts tot the humanitarian visa scheme.

Earlier comments from the government left the door open for cuts.

The Albanese government has denied plans to slash Australia’s humanitarian intake by a third, after reports the cut was being considered as part of a broader push to reduce net overseas migration.

On Thursday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement the government's 20,000 humanitarian placements would "be continued in future years, consistent with Australia’s humanitarian commitments".

The statement followed reporting on Thursday morning by The Australian Financial Review newspaper that Labor appeared poised to reduce humanitarian placements from 20,000 to 13,750 at the start of the next financial year and that it had factored the decrease into migration forecasts.

A spokesman for Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told SBS News earlier on Thursday that the final decision on next year's humanitarian intake had not yet been made and linked the process to next year's budget. At the time he did not rule out cuts.

But in his statement to SBS News, Albanese said the existing figure "remains government policy".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In the wake of multiple international conflicts around the world, Labor has made a series of increases to the humanitarian intake, pushing it to its current high.

The confusion comes as the government is anticipated to announce an overhaul of its migration policy.

Labor had been expected to reveal details in a National Press Club address by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke earlier this month, but the speech was cancelled after Burke failed to secure cabinet agreement on the best approach.

Since then, Albanese has refused to give further updates, telling ABC radio on Tuesday that there are a "series of plans in place" but there is still "more work to do" to finalise them. He declined to set a timeframe for immigration announcements, saying only that they would come at "appropriate times".

Migration targets have been the source of recent public debate, with One Nation pushing a tough anti-migration stance and gaining in the polls.

Both major parties have sought to restrict their own immigration policies while denying that this is in response to the minor party's growing popularity.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has said the Coalition will cap net overseaos migration (NOM) at or below the number of homes built in Australia the previous year. Current building rates suggest their figure would be under 180,000; however, the Coalition is yet to announce where they would restrict immigration to reach that figure.

In 2024-2025, NOM was 306,000. Labor's budgetary forecasts suggest it will decline to 225,000 by 2027-2028, after the party has made concerted efforts to bring it down from a post-pandemic peak of 568,000.

One Nation has stated its preferred migration target is 130,000, although One Nation MP David Farley claimed the party would accept an additional 100,000 essential workers at the weekend. Party leader Pauline Hanson and MP Barnaby Joyce soon corrected him in a public fallout over targets.

What is Labor planning?

According to a report by The Australian newspaper on Wednesday, Labor is close to finalising its immigration crackdown, which will restrict international students and their families and limit visitor visas.

Burke is expected to reveal sweeping changes within weeks, with some measures thought to take effect in September.

The student visa changes could stop internationals from changing courses to extend their stay, reject onshore visa applications, limit the number of family members allowed on the visas, and halt the transfer of people from higher education into vocational or training programs.

Certain tourist visas are also expected to be cut from 12 months down to six.

READ MORE The long wait for permanency in Australia's shrinking humanitarian program

The changes follow already substantial immigration reductions.

Australia's permanent migration program was brought down from a post-pandemic high of 195,000 to 185,000.

In July, the skilled visa program was overhauled, pushing overseas applicants to the back of the queue to slow the pace of new arrivals.

In addition, graduate visas have become more expensive, with lower age limits and stricter English-language requirements. Proof-of-funds requirements were also raised for international students to clamp down on illegal work.

While no government can dictate a net overseas migration (NOM) figure — a measurement of human movement, not a quota — it can adjust visas and entry requirements which impact NOM.

While Labor ministers are concerned that a more hardline approach to immigration will see them lose left-wing voter support, they are thought to be trying to ensure that the government can at least meet its own immigration forecasts.

title: A landmark US deal could change social media forever
text:
In brief Meta has reached a settlement with 29 US states that had taken it to court.

The terms of the settlement will see Meta radically alter its Facebook and Instagram platforms to limit how teenagers can use them.

Meta Platforms will pay up to US$18 billion ($25 billion) over the next decade and strictly limit how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram under an agreement with nearly all 50 US states that took it to trial to resolve claims it designed those social media platforms to addict children.

The settlements announced on Wednesday end a federal trial over allegations Meta's products harmed children, and the company misled the public about their safety. Four of the states — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey — were expected to seek close to US$200 billion ($279 billion) in civil penalties.

While Meta will not undergo a fundamental overhaul, the accords represent a sweeping effort to define how it serves young users.

It could provide a template for resolving thousands of other lawsuits against social media companies. Governments around the world are trying to curb children's access to harmful online content, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.

“The focus of this case was to protect our kids," Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser said in a statement. "The relief we are getting in this settlement is very meaningful and well beyond what any court has ordered or is likely to order."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Meta agreed over the next decade to restrict teenagers' use of Facebook and Instagram to two hours a day and block all usage from midnight to 6am, absent parental consent.

These limits could be tightened if the social media platforms Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube adopt similar terms. Meta will also disable most push notifications to teenage users during school hours of 8am to 3pm and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content.

The settlement does not require Meta to abandon personalised recommendations or targeted advertising. It also does not address some content Meta researchers found particularly problematic, including posts that made Instagram users uncomfortable with their body image.

Meta denied wrongdoing in agreeing to settle. The total payout represents about three to four months of profit and about one month of revenue for Meta.

READ MORE These young women call for social media companies to better protect the safety of young diverse women online

"Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta," the Menlo Park, California-based company said in a blog post. "We want to get this right for parents and teens."

Changing the online experience

Meta agreed to make maximum payments of about US$16.7 billion ($22 billion) to 47 U.S. states, Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

California could receive a US$2.2 billion ($3 billion) payout, while New York could receive US$1.1 billion ($1.5 billion). Texas reached a separate settlement worth more than US$1 billion ($1.3 billion).

Some states will deposit funds in general accounts, while others will earmark portions to address children's mental health.

"This is a big deal," said James Speta, a Northwestern University law professor who specialises in telecommunications and internet policy.

"Meta and other companies were facing pressure to change business practices whether or not they lost the lawsuits, from the public and from Congress and state legislatures," he continued. "These restrictions will change the experience on Instagram and Facebook, and they are designed to reduce engagement."

The settlement includes guaranteed payments of about US$12.7 billion ($17.7 billion), with another US$5 billion ($6.9 billion) contingent on whether Snap Inc's Snapchat, ByteDance's TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube impose similar protections for children.

Those companies were not immediately available for comment. Meta plans to publish a letter on Friday in national newspapers to push TikTok and YouTube to improve protections for children. A Meta spokesperson said the company was "hopeful" Snap would make similar changes.

Thursday's settlements also call for Meta to pay US$459 million ($640 million) to resolve states' privacy claims related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where a British consulting firm collected personal data of millions of Facebook users without authorisation.

US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers approved the main settlement early Thursday. She had overseen the trial that began on 18 August.

At a hearing, she called the settlement "a good step forward," and told lawyers for Meta and the states: "I am quite happy to not have to finish up this trial."

Instagram head Adam Mosseri had begun testifying before the settlement was announced, and Meta Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg had been expected to testify.

Mosseri told representatives of the states last month that Meta would appeal any verdict it lost but would make constructive changes if a settlement could be worked out, people familiar with the matter said.

Mental health crisis

Social media companies still face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities claiming they knowingly sought to addict children and caused a mental health crisis, including harms such as anxiety, depression and suicide. Gonzalez Rogers oversees many of these cases.

The Meta trial included claims by California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey that the company's conduct violated state consumer protection laws.

It also included claims by 29 states that Meta ⁠violated the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act by knowingly collecting personal data from children without parental consent, and using the data to train generative AI.

Meta had long argued that it could not have misled consumers because "social media addiction" was not a recognised psychiatric condition.

Before the trial began, Meta said California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were seeking up to US$1.4 trillion ($1.9 trillion) in penalties.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay US$567 million ($790 million) and implement youth safety measures, in addition to US$375 million ($523 million) a jury ordered Meta to pay in the same case in March for misleading users about its platforms' safety.

Also in March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Alphabet's Google negligent in designing their platforms, and ordered them to pay US$6 million ($8.3 million) to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child.

Meta and Google have said they will appeal those verdicts.

Last month, the European Commission threatened to fine Meta unless it changed some product features, after preliminarily finding that the company breached a 2022 European Union regulation governing the removal of harmful content by large online platforms. A spokesperson said the commission remains in dialogue with Meta on possible changes.

New Mexico was not part of Wednesday's settlements.

Raul Torrez, the New Mexico attorney general, said the resolution missed some changes his case spurred in his state, including safeguards against adults targeting children and banning sexualized AI chatbot interactions with children, yet "represents real progress and adds momentum to finish the job of protecting kids online."

Florida also did not settle and plans to keep litigating.

"The payouts to the states are peanuts compared to the profound harms Meta’s profit-driven addictive features have inflicted on our children," Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said in a statement. "We’ll see them at trial."

title: Australia is being urged to join a $41 trillion fight playing out in its backyard
text:
In Brief China and the United States are in a race to start deep-sea mining critical minerals in the Pacific Ocean.

The issue has starkly divided Pacific nations, with many opposed to deep-sea mining and some in favour.

Sitting at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean are vast deposits of the critical minerals that could drive a potential green transition.

The race to start mining these deposits has begun, and experts say what happens next could impact Australia's relationship with once-reliable Pacific allies.

Commercial deep-sea mining in the Pacific has been on the cards for many years, but the not-yet-existent industry had been on pause while a United Nations agency responsible for the ocean floor develops guidelines for extraction.

That changed last year when United States President Donald Trump's administration took the controversial step of issuing an executive order allowing US companies to apply for licences in its Pacific territories, sidestepping international law.

One US company has publicly committed to start operations as soon as 2027, and in August the US shocked Pacific island communities by announcing it planned to auction off a maritime territory near American Samoa for deep-sea mining.

In 2025, China signed a deal with the Cook Islands to co-operate on seabed mineral development and research and is reportedly considering a similar partnership with Kiribati.

Now the US and China are locked in a geopolitical battle in the Pacific to corner the industry — valued at up to US$30 trillion ($41.88 trillion) — before it's even begun.

Deep-sea mining operations are designed to vacuum polymetallic nodules off the ocean floor. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

The subject has starkly divided Pacific nations. Some want to cash in on the new mining boom, while others worry the largely untested industry could wreak havoc on the environment.

Experts warn this division could leave the region vulnerable to exploitation and damage Australia's relations with its closest regional partners.

What is deep-sea mining?

Deep-sea mining as an industry does not yet exist, but the technology behind it does, and countries have been surveying the ocean floor for years to understand what kinds of deposits lie at the bottom of the ocean.

These deposits come in several forms, but extracting so-called 'polymetallic nodules' forms the backbone of existing deep-sea mining technology.

Naoero (formally Nauru), the Cook Islands, Tonga and Kiribati support deep-sea mining, while the remaining members of the Pacific Islands Forum oppose it. Source: SBS News

Formed layer by layer, over millions of years, these potato-sized forms are found between 3,500 and 6,500 metres beneath the surface.

To extract these deposits, a large harvesting vehicle drives across the pitch-black ocean floor, vacuuming up the deposits and the surface layer of sediment before pumping the material to the surface via a pipe for sorting.

What does this have to do with Australia?

The Lowy Institute's Connor Graham told SBS News Australia has two key reasons to be concerned about deep-sea mining in the Pacific.

The first is political.

The issue has starkly divided Pacific nations. Naoero (formally Nauru), the Cook Islands, Tonga and Kiribati support the emerging industry, while the remaining members of the Pacific Islands Forum have come out in strong opposition.

"If deep-sea mining divides the Pacific into two camps, then we will see a breakdown in that unity that has historically defined the Pacific, and that could be a destabilising force that could leave Pacific nations vulnerable to external influences," Graham said.

"Say Kiribati signs a deal with China to mine. They become aligned with Beijing. They're still a member of the Pacific Islands Forum, but now more influenced by Beijing than they currently are."

READ MORE The multi-billion-dollar question that could pit Australia and its neighbours against each other

Graham said Australia should play "moderator" and advocate for a Pacific-led governance framework for deep-sea mining that would provide all Pacific nations with clear, baseline standards for any deep-sea exploration.

"It would outline minimum expectations for environmental protections, remediation and revenue sharing," he said.

"At the moment, nothing like that exists, leaving these countries vulnerable to bad deals — companies will go wherever governance is weakest. A strong framework protects all countries equally."

He said the second issue was environmental.

What are the environmental concerns?

Graham said scientists were "very concerned" that deep-sea mining could have "profound" impacts on the delicate and largely mysterious ecosystems at the bottom of the ocean. Scientists believe they have only described 5 per cent of the life at depths where this mining would take place.

The potato-shaped nodules are the only solid forms on the sea floor, and are home to sponges, corals, crustaceans and worms, which would lose their only habitats if they were removed. The consequences of this are not fully understood.

The mining process also involves pumping sediment from the sea floor to the surface and then pumping it back into water 1,000m below the surface — moving nutrients and fine particles with it.

"There are pretty big concerns about how much this will impact the fisheries in the Pacific — these plumes won't care about the borders of your exclusive economic zone. It could just sort of float around off into next door and impact fisheries in a massive area," Graham said.

Naoero is one of several Pacific nations hoping to profit from the deep-sea mining boom. Source: Getty / Xinhua News Agency

He said this environmental impact could further destabilise the region.

"If one country's deep-sea mining ruined another fishery, that would have a serious political consequence," he said.

Graham said deep-sea mining also raised questions about carbon storage. Scientists are concerned disruptions to deep-sea algae could change how much carbon they can store, and disturbing them could accelerate climate change.

All about politics

Susan Park is an international relations expert from the University of Sydney.

She told SBS News it was important to situate deep-sea mining in the broader geopolitical race for the Pacific.

Deep-sea mining operations would bring infrastructure and political relationships with the countries that host them.

"China and the US want to maintain their control and influence in the Pacific — it's about shipping lanes and access," Park said.

Susan Park said the race to mine the deep sea needed to be understood in the broader race to control the Pacific. Source: Supplied

Park also pointed out that while these critical minerals were extremely important, geologists are "confident we have enough of them on the Earth's surface", raising further questions about the need to develop the new industry.

A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said Australia would not support deep-sea mining in areas beyond national jurisdiction until there was a "comprehensive and robust regulatory framework in place, negotiated through the International Seabed Authority (ISA) in accordance with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

"As a member of the ISA Council, Australia is working with partners to negotiate a regulatory framework that ensures assessment of potential environmental impacts based on scientific evidence, includes strong environmental protections, and establishes robust inspection, compliance and enforcement mechanisms."

title: It was Dolly Parton's proudest legacy. Now an Australian town must keep it alive
text:
In Brief Dolly Parton's Imagination Library has delivered more than two million books across Australia.

But those in regional areas say more financial help is needed to keep the initiative alive.

In the regional NSW city of Tamworth, more than 3,000 children are reading more books because of Dolly Parton — a mark of Australia's connection to the legendary country singer, actor and philanthropist that runs deeper than one might initially think.

Parton died on Wednesday morning at 80. Tributes have poured in from around the world, but in Tamworth, the loss is more personal.

The city, dubbed the country music capital of Australia, holds an official sister-city bond with Parton's adopted hometown of Nashville and hosted Parton herself on her last Australian tour in 2014.

"It's an incredible nod to us that she would come here when most stars are looking for the big 70,000-seater auditoriums, whereas ours is 5,000 seats," Cheryl Brown, from the Tamworth Country Music Festival, told SBS News.

"So for her to come here, she certainly validated us as the country music capital and that saw us being an important part of country music here in Australia."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The Imagination Library was Dolly Parton's proudest philanthropic venture — and its "gold star" pupil is in regional NSW. Source: Supplied / Tamworth Regional Council

But it's her gift of the Imagination Library program, one of Parton's most personal philanthropic projects, that has really transformed Tamworth.

Founded in 1995 as a tribute to her illiterate father, Dolly Parton's Imagination Library is a free book-gifting program — now running across the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Ireland, and Australia — that mails new, age-appropriate books to children from birth until they turn five, completely free of charge.

It has gifted more than 300 million books to children since it started 31 years ago. In Australia, more than two million of those books have been delivered to 151,000 children across 480 communities since its launch here in 2013.

Dolly's 'gold star' pupil

In Tamworth, where the program has run since 2019, its ambassador Lisa Rennie says it has fundamentally changed how children relate to reading and literacy.

"Children from birth to the age of five are eligible to receive the books, which are chosen by qualified speech pathologists and early literacy teachers," Rennie told SBS News.

"There are currently about 3,500 children on average on the program in the Tamworth region."

Since 2019, more than 98 per cent of children born in Tamworth have been enrolled.

"We've been classed the gold star program," Rennie said.

Families sign up at no cost, ensuring accessibility for those experiencing disadvantage — books are posted to each home each month, and caregivers are also given reading guidance sheets to help foster lifelong reading in families.

About 70 per cent of those books are by Australian authors and 10 per cent by First Nations authors.

Research from United Way Australia, which delivers the program in Australia, found children involved in the program in Tamworth were being read to more often, for longer, and had more books in the home than the average Australian child.

The Imagination Library has transformed Tamworth's literacy, with 98 per cent of children born there being enrolled in the program. Source: Supplied / Tamworth Regional Council

They were also significantly more likely to demonstrate emerging literacy skills, with Rennie expecting that, as graduates of the program enter primary school, they will show an increased level of literacy reflected in NAPLAN results in the region.

"Children in our region are being read to more often, for longer, and if they're on the program for the full five years, they're receiving a whole library of 60 books that they can cherish," she said.

"There's more people visiting our local libraries, which is fantastic, which is purely as a result of this program," she adds.

United Way CEO Dr Lyndsey McKee says Parton started the program as a response to her own upbringing in a family that experienced poverty.

"Her father was illiterate and she was one of 12, so she didn't have access to opportunities that many children have," McKee told SBS News. "With that lived experience, she really wanted to bring storytelling to the world."

"It's a huge legacy beyond her singing ... she's such an incredible philanthropist."

Keeping the legacy going

In lieu of flowers, Parton's family has asked for donations to be made to the Imagination Library.

It's a request that carries extra weight in Australia: the Imagination Library is the only program of its kind in the country, and it could sit in a precarious financial position, particularly amid Parton's death.

The program operates through a shared funding model with The Dollywood Foundation, Parton's charity organisation, and United Way Australia.

But the costs of running the program are left to the community.

"United Way send the books out, but we arrange the funding here locally with fundraisers and sponsorships from local businesses, council, local clubs, and even individuals reach out to give the gift of literacy," Rennie explained.

In July, US singer-songwriter Taylor Swift and her husband Travis Kelce donated US$2 million ($2.78 million) to the Imagination Library as part of a wider round of wedding-week giving — but that kind of support doesn't necessarily flow through to the grassroots costs faced by groups like Tamworth's.

Lisa Rennie is calling for more financial support to keep Dolly Parton's program — and legacy — alive. Source: Supplied / Tamworth Regional Council

Those costs add up. Each book delivered costs $9 per child per month.

In somewhere like Tamworth, that equates to just under $400,000 a year required to keep every eligible child enrolled.

McKee said there's an "absolute need" for Parton's program in Australia.

"Twenty per cent of children are starting school developmentally vulnerable. One in three children in the recent NAPLAN results were not meeting the reading benchmark."

"The evidence says this program works.

"We want to use this important moment to actually do more and bring this program to more children and communities in the years ahead."

Brown says Dolly will "be on the streets of Tamworth forever" as a result of the program.

"It's a wonderful gift that Dolly has given to us here in Tamworth, and we will certainly endeavour to carry that on forever," she said.

READ MORE How Dolly Parton is fostering a love of reading in children around Australia

Rennie says it's even more important that donations continue to flow through the program following Parton's death.

"The Tamworth region will be forever grateful for Dolly Parton introducing this program to Australia," she said.

"But I think now more than ever, this program needs to continue because it'll be in her legacy.

"We need the financial support to ensure that it does continue."

title: A $1.4 billion question: The case for a new tax on Australians
text:
In brief Sugar-sweetened drink consumption could fall 24 per cent if a sugar tax is introduced, new research has found.

The tax could raise revenue for health services and dental care initiatives.

A 20 per cent tax on sugary drinks could prevent millions of tooth cavities and add hundreds of thousands of years to Australians' lives collectively, according to new research,

A Griffith University study published in BMJ Public Health on Wednesday found a levy applied to non-alcoholic drinks with added sugar, such as soft drinks and most juices, could prevent 3.7 million cases of tooth decay, 191,000 cases of gum disease, and 115,000 cases of complete tooth loss across Australia over the next 25 years.

The study suggested that tax revenue could be used to strengthen health services and to implement a universal health care approach to dental care, but co-author Lennert Veerman said the benefits would extend beyond oral health.

"The study also estimates a 20 per cent sugar tax would generate approximately half a million health-adjusted life years for the 2019 Australian population over their lifetime, both from dental health improvements and reductions in weight-related illness," the Griffith University public health professor said.

As of 2017–2018, approximately 9.1 per cent of Australians adults reported drinking sugar-sweetened beverages every day, while nearly one-third of Australians aged 15 and older had untreated tooth decay or cavities, according to the study.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Using a computer-based simulation, researchers found that for every 1 per cent increase in the price of sugar-sweetened drinks, consumption was expected to drop by 1.2 per cent.

Assuming a 20 per cent tax is passed on in full to consumers, the study predicted the price increase would result in a 24 per cent reduction in consumption.

Marco Peres from SingHealth Duke-NUS in Singapore said the findings highlighted the oral health benefits of sugar taxes.

"Importantly, a sugar tax is a population-level measure," he said.

"It does not rely solely on individuals changing their behaviour but helps create an environment in which healthier choices become easier.

"This is particularly important if we want prevention strategies to reach the whole population and reduce health inequalities."

United Kingdom tax reduced sugar content

Oral diseases are a growing public health concern, affecting approximately 3.5 billion people globally.

The study found that oral diseases contributed to 2.4 per cent of Australia’s total health burden — the impact of a health problem on a population — and ranked among the top 10 diseases.

According to the World Health Organization, 116 countries have an excise tax on at least one type of sugar-sweetened beverage. The study notes there is a high level of support among the Australian public for policies that reduce sugar intake.

In 2018, the United Kingdom introduced a tax of 19.4 or 25.9 pence per litre, depending on the sugar content of beverages.

It led to a 46 per cent reduction in the sugar contained in soft drinks, the UK government said, with nearly 90 per cent of the market now containing sugar below the level at which the tax applies.

A 2024 parliamentary inquiry into Australia's diabetes epidemic recommended Australia introduce a 20 per cent tax on sugar-sweetened drinks.

The Parliamentary Budget Office estimated that, after allowing for collection costs and a drop in GST revenue, such a tax would raise nearly $1.4 billion in the following two financial years.

At the time, the Australian Medical Association said it was "100 per cent behind" the tax.

"Our modelling shows we can prevent thousands of cases of diabetes if we act," the association's president Steve Robson said.

In 2024, the Australian Beverages Council — the peak body for the non-alcoholic drinks industry in the country — rejected calls for a sugar tax, claiming it was a "misguided measure that misses the mark and will only hit hardest those households that can least afford it".

While critics argue a sugar tax would disproportionately affect lower-income households, a 2017 Deakin University study found those households stood to gain the greatest health benefits.

4 Pines Park: The one thing Manly fans were looking forward did not happen on Friday evening. The Sea Eagles thumped a woeful St George Illawarra 44-10 to keep their slim finals hopes alive. Loading Manly simply need to beat the New Zealand Warriors next weekend and rely on South Sydney or the Cowboys losing both of their final two games to qualify. The Sea Eagles have the firepower and confidence to cause some headaches should they make it to September.

Advertisement

Who would want to stop Haumole Olakau’atu in full flight? Tom Trbojevic is two games back from a hamstring injury and also bound to strip fitter. And what about Clayton Faulolo, who bagged a try, set up another three and is proving arguably the best utility on the northern beaches? But the 13,957 supporters inside 4 Pines Park one last time this season, including members of the club’s 1996 premiership team, rose to their feet for the kick-off in the 74th minute when Nathan Brown was ready to launch himself off the back fence. Brown was playing his 200th NRL game and his last at home before finishing his career in the Super League next year. What Brown lacks in size he makes up for in heart, and quickly earned the reputation for his kick-off carries, not to mention the nickname “Back-fence Brown”.

Advertisement

The TV cameras captured Brown’s eyes light up when the Dragons kicked to his side of the field. The Italian international started to steam on to the ball, got excited, then realised the pass from Jamal Fogarty was never coming because he had dropped the ball. Brown let out a giant sigh, as did the supporters. Departing Manly forward Nathan Brown celebrated his 200th NRL game with a big win. NRL Photos “I felt for him because I saw him wind up about three or four times, he wanted to have one of those carries,” coach Kieran Foran said. “He’s been such a warrior, to get to 200 games and the way he’s had to do it – he’s stayed in the fight a long time – it was great to see him go out a winner [at home] tonight.” It was a shame, but it was never going to change the result.

Advertisement

As is the case every year, Manly are the one club teams above them probably do not want to meet in the finals. If they fall short, they will rue a few tight losses, including golden-point defeats to Canterbury and the Cowboys. It is still a success, considering they dropped their opening three games, sacked coach Anthony Seibold, then eventually appointed one of their favourite sons, Foran, to succeed him. Things will become a lot clearer about the September hopes in the next few days. The future looks bright, regardless, when you think of a player like Faulolo, as well as Onitoni Large, who made his debut with 20 minutes remaining, and was given a warm embrace by Trbojevic as he took the field.

Large is just 19, was in the Wests Tigers system before signing a three-year deal with Manly, and was just as handy at rugby. Foran is confident he has a big future: “The thing I love about Onitoni [during] the last six weeks is the growth we’ve seen in his game; we felt like he was so ready if he was called upon. He’s going to be a special player. He’s young, raw, but he works hard on his game.” Josh Feledy keeps the points coming for the Sea Eagles on Friday night. Getty Images The Sea Eagles were given a standing ovation when they led 26-0 at the break against a Dragons side that completed only 10 of their 15 sets. Things did not improve for the men wearing red and white in the second half. The Dragons will finish with the wooden spoon. At least they have recruited well and have plenty to get excited about in 2027. Still, they will want to finish on a high next week on home soil, and send out the likes of the departing Damien Cook on a high.

At last decentralisation is being raised as a solution to manage Melbourne’s burgeoning housing crisis. Access to good-quality, affordable housing is fundamental to society, but the short-term solutions of the Victorian government only compromise our long-term future. The Whitlam government began a program of decentralisation, developing cities like Albury-Wodonga. If these policies had not been abandoned by the Fraser government, Melbourne would be a much more liveable city today. With Melbourne’s population set to grow to more than 10 million by 2101, the priority should be to secure quality of life, the environment, jobs and prosperity for future generations. Decentralisation is complex, long term, expensive and difficult to implement, but the prospects of infinite growth are simply unsustainable, and show poor regard for future generations. If planning encompassed all of Victoria, redirecting growth towards regional cities rather than just its capital, it could ultimately restore Melbourne’s status as the world’s most liveable city.

Bryan Long, Balwyn Climate resilience must play a factor

It is helpful to understand the nuts and bolts of Melbourne on track for megacity status: How will it cope? But equally important is understanding the sustainable-living implications of where we are heading. Climate change is no longer a future problem. Melbourne is already experiencing hotter, drier and more volatile conditions, with growing risks from extreme heat, drought, flooding, water scarcity and declining urban tree canopy and biodiversity. These risks become more significant as it moves towards a population of up to 10 million. Greater density and development will intensify pressure on water, energy, open space, sporting facilities and urban cooling. The question is whether our planning framework is adequately integrating climate resilience into the decisions shaping this future. Climate, biodiversity, water and urban forest policies mean little if they do not influence statutory planning and development decisions.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly Looking outside growth for answers

The word ″⁣cope″⁣ in the heading ″⁣Melbourne on track for megacity status: How will it cope?″⁣ (28/8) is revealing. I could cope with becoming overweight. But it would force me to spend much of my budget on new clothes, and damage my health. Being able to cope is not a criterion for wisdom. The same goes for urban planning. The infrastructure needed to cope with Melbourne’s historic growth has blown the government’s budget. And the congestion on our roads in our schools and hospitals, and the loss of green spaces have lessened our well-being. I cannot see us even reducing the infrastructure backlog – just to maintain services, not improve them – while Melbourne keeps growing. When will the penny drop that ″⁣growth″⁣ is not a solution? It is one of the drivers of so many problems. As Monash University’s Dr Taylor says, ″⁣There has to be more to planning than just growth.″⁣

Ian Penrose, Kew

Advertisement

THE FORUM Perils of AI

The article “Gates warns global leaders on risks of AI” (28/8) highlights the profound risks of this technology to us all. Why then are our parliamentarians so enthusiastic about it? Where are the safeguards? Have they knowledge of how to control it unbeknown to Bill Gates? His comment, “We don’t have to adapt to it because it can adapt to us”, says it all.

Christine Baker, Rosanna AI guardrails

The article ″⁣Albanese tells Queensland to toe the line on AI″⁣ (26/8) on emerging bipartisan support for AI is encouraging, but allowing more data centres is not an economic strategy by itself. Australia should welcome AI investment on clear conditions. Data centre operators must pay for the electricity infrastructure they require, bring additional clean and reliable power into the grid, protect Australian data and provide local training and employment.

The greater challenge is what happens beyond the data centres. AI will remove routine tasks from administration, recruitment, accounting, law and customer service. It may not eliminate entire occupations immediately, but it could quietly remove the entry-level jobs through which people gain experience.

Government should require transparency and human review when AI affects hiring, pay or dismissal. Workers displaced by technology should receive practical retraining, income support and temporary wage insurance while moving into new fields.

Australia should neither stop AI nor subsidise it blindly. We should adopt it confidently while ensuring the companies receiving the productivity gains also carry the infrastructure, environmental and social costs.

Daryl Keeley, Hawthorn East Glacial action

The Himalayas are sometimes referred to as “the third pole” because of the huge amount of ice storage. But because of rising global temperatures, Nepal has lost about a third of its glacial coverage over the past three decades.

With rising temperatures there will be more glacier collapses and with them the sickening devastation being seen. Over time reduced water flows from glacial melts will also result in water shortages for the billions who live downstream in Nepal and India. That will inevitably result in massive numbers of climate refugees, desperate for a more liveable environment.

Nepal has contributed almost nothing to the climate crisis, less than 0.1 per cent of global emissions a year. Meanwhile Australia, as the world’s second-largest exporter of fossil fuels, is a major contributor. And we’re still arguing about net zero and whether we should develop our renewables sector? Where is our humanity?

Peter Cook, Essendon What of our stance?

As reporter Nick O’Malley reports, “whatever the proximate cause, there is broad agreement that climate change is the catalysing force” behind the mudslide in the Himalayas (″⁣A terrifying mass of ice, mud, water, debris and rock: How disaster unfolded″⁣, 28/8). It is heartbreaking enough to watch this tragedy unfold, but particularly galling to know that in the midst of escalating climate catastrophes, the Albanese government is preparing to approve yet another coal mine extension and has backpedalled to allow coal and gas to power hyperscale data centres. With the Pacific Islands Forum next week, and Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen soon to preside over negotiations at this year’s global climate conference, COP31, Australia’s stance matters. How will a nation that remains one of the world’s largest exporters of polluting coal and gas, be viewed by Pacific nations and the wider international community?

Amy Hiller, Kew

Advertisement

More than talk needed

How many years have we been talking about climate change and the effects of not taking charge to make changes? Instead we keep taking and abusing the planet.

In recent years we have experienced devastating fires, floods, landslides, drought, volcanos erupting. All causing loss of human lives, wildlife, livestock and environmental devastation. The latest in Nepal. Governments talk, nations sign agreements but nothing happens. Most of us have children, grandchildren, family. Is this the world we want them to live in? Why should they be responsible for what impotent governments are not doing?

Jane Taylor, Newport Laughed, and cried

I shall miss my daily dose of humour from the pen of Cathy Wilcox. Cathy’s cartoons have made me laugh, cry, ashamed and guilty, and always, always thought-provoking. Enjoy smelling the roses Cathy, breakfast will not be the same without you.

Veronica Paskins, Somers Making sense

Farewell Cathy Wilcox and thanks for the art. Your work made sense of the tragic and ludicrous times we live in. Your insightful and fearless representations brought a smile to my face in the mornings and helped me get through the day. It will be harder to read The Age knowing you won’t be there.

Rohan Wightman, Brunswick The sad farewell

Unlike your other cartoons Cathy Wilcox, your farewell one on Friday left me quite sad. All the best for the the future and thanks for giving me so much pleasure.

Ron Mather, Melbourne Nailed the issues

Thank you Cathy Wilcox – the best and bravest cartoonist in Australia. You nailed it every time, whatever the issue, be it Gaza, the climate crisis, the femicide epidemic, or the need for real tax reform.

You’ll be sorely missed.

Anne Lewis, Northcote

Advertisement

Giving thanks

Cathy Wilcox thanked readers in her last cartoon (28/8), but I think we must all thank her.

Her incisive wit has helped many of us come to terms with so many fraught issues for nearly four decades. She will be missed by so many of us. Thank you for the laughs, the often cryptic, clever responses, but more especially, thank you for forcing us to delve a little more into issues from a different perspective.

Sally Davis, Malvern East A great privilege

For so long, Cathy Wilcox encouraged readers to grapple with such a wide range of issues and helped us to deal with potential outcomes. Her drawings were either so deceptively simple or made us read the text over and over. Thank you Cathy, it has been the greatest privilege to read your creations.

Judith Hudson, Elwood A day ruined

Oh no! My day is ruined. Cathy Wilcox is heading off to wherever brilliant, incisive, hilarious cartoonists go when they ″⁣take a break″⁣. Her dyslexic cow meditating is coming with me in my mind’s third eye as I head into a yoga class. Thank you and best wishes.

Jane Ross, San Remo Decentralised, again

Interesting that decentralisation is being discussed again after a long hiatus. In the 1970s, I worked on a decentralisation scheme run by Victoria, NSW and the Whitlam government in a rare spirit of co-operation. The growth centres for Victoria were Portland, Ballarat, Bendigo, Albury-Wodonga and the Latrobe Valley. The population of Melbourne was a shade under 2 million. After the Fraser government took office in 1975 the scheme was allowed to fade away. It seemed an odd decision coming from a Western District farmer in coalition with a rural-based party.

Ken Turnbull, Maldon Joy of words

I cannot conceive of a world where people cannot read or write, and yet even in this day and age, such people exist. Getting lost in a fantasy world of literature is surely one of the greatest gifts one can have.

Marie Nash, Balwyn

Advertisement

Trump’s lochjaw

The Donald Trump may be losing his grip, renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America, when clearly he intended it to be Lake Trump.

James Ogilvie, Kew Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Wilcox

Cathy Wilcox has been the best at ″⁣the best job in the world″⁣. She will be sorely missed.

Betty Rudin, Wandin North

Advertisement

Mornings will not be the same without Cathy Wilcox. Her cartoons have made me think, laugh and usually nod my head and say, “Spot on Cathy, you’re a treasure.“

Les Cooper, Anglesea Cathy Wilcox’s cartoons were part of my morning. No one else could capture my thoughts on life and the state of the world so simply and so beautifully. Enjoy your well-deserved break, Cathy.

Anne Wood, Birregurra Cartoonists like Cathy Wilcox are a gift to society who thankfully can’t, and won’t, be muzzled.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton How deeply distressing to find Cathy Wilcox is parking her pencils. I will truly miss her insightful and amusing work.

Paul Dover, Canterbury Trump

Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario Lake America. He has no need to attack Canada, as most Canadians have died laughing.

Mike Francis, Fitzroy

No matter how often Donald Trump demands, I will still come from Woorinen North.

Barrie Bales, Woorinen North Furthermore

Brand new road near Kyneton, built from base up, was finished a few weeks ago. Now after some rain it has potholes. Something is wrong with our road construction technique. Please fix it.

Michelle Leeder, Trentham I don’t mind paying taxes (or a levy) for government projects, but I do mind my contribution being spent inefficiently.

Kevan Porter, Alphington A robot can run faster than Usain Bolt, yet Bolt knew how and when to stop!

The scariest book to read in 2026 is 1984.

title: From the hand of Dan: A secret tax, a handwritten note, and a hard lesson for Ben Carroll
text:
Ben Carroll has kept a handwritten note from Daniel Andrews as a reminder of how not to govern.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ben Carroll was sitting in his Bali hotel room on a family holiday when he received a call from a journalist seeking confirmation on a big story – that the Melbourne Airport Rail Link, a major infrastructure project close to Carroll’s heart, had been shelved. Carroll was adamant the Herald Sun reporter had gotten the wrong end of the stick. “You’re completely wrong,” he told him. “I’m the public transport minister. It goes through my electorate. We took this to the 2022 election. I would know about it.” The following day, the paper duly splashed with the news that the project had been mothballed, ostensibly due to concerns about the state’s rising debt. Carroll was furious. He was later informed, through a three-way telephone conversation with then treasurer Tim Pallas and deputy premier Jacinta Allan, that the decision had indeed been made, in secret and without his knowledge, by the Expenditure Review Committee, a meeting of four senior ministers chaired by Daniel Andrews. Then-premier Jacinta Allan with Ben Carroll in May. Eddie Jim It was a Saturday morning in April 2023, in the final months of the Andrews government. Two days later, Carroll was back at work in his usual spot around the cabinet table and still steaming. Andrews, sensing the heat rising from his minister, wrote a message on a sticky note and passed it to Carroll. “We’ve got the sequence (at last) right on MARL,” it read.

Advertisement

More than three years later, Carroll still has the note pinned above his desk as a reminder of how not to govern. The story is well known among the new premier’s trusted circle, two of whom relayed it to The Age, both for what it says about the secretive, highly centralised way in which Andrews ran the state, and Carroll’s determination to do things differently if he ever got the chance. It also helps explain why Carroll was genuinely outraged when he this week discovered, through the meticulous reporting of the Victorian Auditor General’s Office, the full, malodorous history of the Rail Improvement Charge (RIC), a hidden levy on public transport users that has sat on the state’s books – or rather, off book – since the start of last year. Related Article Suburban Rail Loop How Allan, ministers decided to hide public transport levy in secret talks The auditor-general’s report was tabled in parliament on Wednesday, when Carroll was in Sydney for a meeting of national cabinet. He was briefed on its contents but reserved judgement until he read the full report. That happened the next morning when he rose early, printed off its 170 pages at home and scoured it cover to cover. A short time later, he drove into parliament and announced that he was scrapping the RIC and apologised for the entire episode. “There was no transparency on the creation and implementation of this charge,” he said. The RIC, a 1 per cent levy on top of all public transport fares conceived as a new revenue source to finance the Suburban Rail Loop, came into force on January 1 last year and was forecast to funnel $8 billion into government coffers over the next 36 years.

Advertisement

Its sudden death, so shortly after the belated news of its birth, punches a hole in the government’s capacity to service its debt splurge on major infrastructure and raises further doubts about the financial viability of the state’s largest transport construction project, the SRL. The auditor-general’s report – an audit to determine whether the SRL East, the first stage of the 90-kilometre Suburban Rail Loop, is progressing within the government’s stated time frame and budget – does more than trace the history of a curious little tax. Through its forensic account, and The Age’s subsequent conversations with ministers, MPs and bureaucrats who were not authorised to speak publicly, it opens a window on a much deeper problem – the culture of secrecy and control that infected the Andrews and Allan governments. The question it raises for voters in the lead up to the state election is whether they believe that Carroll and his November running mate, Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams, are genuinely committed to greater transparency in government or whether, as long-serving members of the previous administrations, they were part of the problem. Carroll and Gabrielle Williams took charge of the state government last month. Jason South Carroll and Williams have known of the rail charge, though not its full history, since 2024. “There are multiple occasions where the RIC was discussed involving both of them,” one former minister said. “At what point does it stop being incompetence and start to be willful blindness?” Auditor-General Andrew Greaves’s report reveals the charge was conceived five years ago by Pallas and Andrews, in the depths of the COVID crisis, to prop up the investment and business case for the SRL. It was kept secret from all but a small club of senior ministers and departmental officials.

Advertisement

The rail loop business case was published in August 2021, the same month which, according to Greaves, the government first approved a plan to use 60 per cent of RIC revenue – an estimated $4.8 billion between 2025 and 2062 – to repay borrowings for the SRL. More accurately, this is when the plan was approved by the Expenditure Review Committee chaired by Andrews. The other members of the committee were treasurer Pallas, the then minister for the SRL Jacinta Allan and James Merlino, the deputy premier who would go on to chair the Suburban Rail Loop Authority. The decision never went to full cabinet. This is consistent with how Andrews governed. His approach, one borrowed by British Labour luminary Tony Blair, was to elevate a series of subcommittees, all of which he chaired, into discreet, executive forums that operated at arms’ length from cabinet. Sometimes decisions made by subcommittees were reported back to the cabinet, but often they weren’t. Ministers would sometimes be invited to present to subcommittees on matter relating to their portfolio responsibilities, but not always. One former departmental official who sat in on the meetings of one subcommittee said that once a decision was taken, the next order of business would be working out how to tell the minister responsible for overseeing it. Carroll was not alone in learning about a big decision impacting his portfolio on the front page of a newspaper. Decisions of the Andrews government were often not considered by his full cabinet. Jason South

Advertisement

In August 2021, when Andrews and Pallas were nutting out the Rail Improvement Charge, Carroll was the minister for public transport but none the wiser that a new tax on fares was being developed. “I was not part of the creation,” he said this week. Other government ministers told The Age they first heard of the charge when the auditor-general’s report splashed like a brick into the Spring Street pond. “The scales fell from my eyes today,” one current minister said after the report was tabled. Another explained: “You’ve got to remember there was a practice in that previous term of government of putting decisions through the smallest possible collectives of ministers. That was a practice that was started by Daniel and it was continued by Jacinta. What it led to was a complete lack of visibility of policy by the broader cabinet.” The Suburban Rail Loop, a project conceived in secret by private consultants with the knowledge of some of the government’s most senior transport officials, was a product of this culture. The Suburban Rail Loop Authority, the statutory authority created in 2019 to oversee the project, is renowned for the distance it keeps between itself and government departments that overlap with its work. Related Article Public service Thrown in a loop: How Daniel Andrews’ biggest project was cooked up behind closed doors Greaves identifies this problem in his report. He refers to a previously unpublished government review of the authority, which in 2024 raised concerns about “issues with trust, co-operation, information flows and role clarify between the SRLA and central agencies.” Put simply, people on different sides of the SRL wall did not talk to each other. One example of this was a decision taken by the SRLA board to order a pause in negotiations with construction firms over cost over-runs. The board didn’t bother to seek approval from the government for this decision on the management of the state’s largest infrastructure project. A recurring symptom of an unaccountable culture is the frustration expressed by ministerial and departmental staff who tried to get information out of the authority. Two days before the auditor-general’s report was tabled, Carroll announced his intention to wind up the SRLA and fold its functions into another government agency.

title: No govt funds for Bathla as sponsorship terminated, staff stood down
text:
Advertisement

The Western Sydney Wanderers’ sponsorship agreement with a collapsed developer has been terminated, as staff at the company are stood down without pay and the state government remains unconvinced about providing financial assistance. The Wanderers confirmed on Friday its sponsorship agreement with Bathla Group has been terminated. “The club remains in a strong position and is focused on delivering on- and off-field success for our members, fans, partners and the western Sydney community,” the A-league club said in a statement. The Wanderers have terminated a sponsorship agreement with collapsed developer Bathla. Getty Images Bathla Group entered voluntary administration on Tuesday and corporate restructuring agency Teneo was appointed to oversee the company and its hundreds of related entities, including Universal Property Group and Raj & Jai Construction.

Advertisement

Bathla’s collapse adds further pressure to the state government’s housing agenda, which is struggling amid concerns about the feasibility of apartment construction west of Parramatta. The NSW government has been approached for a lifeline but is not yet willing to extend one, lacking a complete picture of the company’s financial position. “The government expects the owners and private creditors to do the right thing,” a state government spokesperson said in a statement on Friday. “Given the circumstances, we are not willing to put taxpayers’ money on the line to guarantee profits for private creditors.” “Our priority is to support the people and small businesses affected by this situation.”

Advertisement

The collapse has left hundreds of buyers who purchased off the plan in limbo, after major developments in Box Hill and Castle Hill were plagued by delays. Work on some western Sydney Bathla projects recently stalled. Tradesmen walked off sites and some said they had not been paid. Some Bathla staff have been stood down without pay ahead of a meeting on Monday morning at the developer’s Girraween headquarters, on which it owes $400,000 in rent. A Bathla construction site at the corner of Cosmos Way and Hynds Road in Box Hill in Sydney’s outer north-west. Janie Barrett As of July, NSW was tracking about 40 per cent behind the rate required to meet the Minns government’s commitment to build 377,000 homes by mid-2029 under the National Housing Accord. Bathla had about 220 construction projects running concurrently – and about 45 of them were in the construction phase – when it entered voluntary administration, the NSW Supreme Court heard on Thursday.

Creditors face a weeks-long wait to find out whether they will get any money back and anxious home buyers have been left in limbo over whether their homes will be completed. Related Article Exclusive

title: There’s one key reason female GPs like me are quitting
text:
Advertisement

NationalHealthcare Opinion There’s one key reason female GPs like me are quitting Elly Goodsall Doctor August 28, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 28, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal government has announced that 84.1 per cent of visits to general practitioners are now bulk billed, and has called that progress. The figure counts the doctors who’ve stayed in the profession. After 13 years, I am not one of them. About four years ago, a patient walked into my consulting room struggling – she told me that much. What she could not yet tell me was that she had a specific plan to end her life, and the means to carry it out. She came back recently to tell me that because of the time and kindness of that first appointment, her children have a mother today. Dr Elly Goodsall, who is quitting as a GP after 13 years in practice, citing the pressures on the “underclass” of female doctors. I have thought about that a great deal. Not with pride, but with the weight of it. She was not describing anything exceptional that I did. She was describing what becomes possible when a GP makes enough time to sit with a person. To notice. To make someone feel that they are worth an hour of another human being’s unhurried attention. That is not a luxury. That is general practice. I am not leaving because I want to. It is the vigilance of never being allowed to miss anything. It is the patient distress carried home. It is the unpaid hours that continue after the last patient has gone. And it is all of that inside a system whose government will not acknowledge, in anything but words, what a good GP is worth. I have been filling the gap between the care I refuse to compromise on and the support I receive to provide it – with my own time, my own earnings, and emotional reserves my children also deserved. I am done.

Advertisement

Female GPs carry a more complex and less remunerated caseload than our male colleagues. In the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners’ 2024 Health of the Nation survey, nearly eight in 10 female GPs named psychological issues among their three most common patient presentations, compared with just over six in 10 male GPs. Women’s health appeared in the top three for 52 per cent of female GPs and 3 per cent of male GPs. Male GPs reported more musculoskeletal, respiratory, circulatory and skin presentations. Complexity takes longer, and it shows: female GPs spend on average three minutes more with every patient. We are also more likely to bulk-bill those who cannot afford to pay, and to run over time because a person needed more than 15 minutes. Related Article Medicare Free GP visits on the rise as 1400 clinics ditch out-of-pocket fees Medicare pays per consultation, not per minute. An analysis by Ochre Health of 511 GPs across its practices found the women billed about $24 an hour less than the men – a gap driven almost entirely by the number of appointments fitted into an hour, not by what women charged. We are not paid less for the same work. We are paid less for more complex work that unavoidably requires more time. The government is telling you that GPs refusing to bulk-bill are the problem. We are not. The problem is an unwillingness to invest meaningfully in general practice, and a determination to disguise that. The “triple bulk-billing incentive” tripled not the bulk-billed rate but a small incentive payment – a pebble thrown into a cavern, with a press release claiming that the cavern was filled and that GPs simply needed to step up. This is not ignorance. Asked at the National Press Club in April whether longer consultations should attract a higher rebate, the minister accepted that female GPs do longer consultations, more mental health work and more complex multi-condition care – but also said he had reached that view on anecdotal evidence, without necessarily seeing the hard data.

Advertisement

I would rather leave than practise Band-Aid medicine. I would earn considerably more doing exactly that – shorter appointments, higher throughput, less emotional investment. The financial logic is obvious. I have never been able to make myself do it. It takes time to build the trust that lets someone finally tell you the thing they have never told anyone. Patients know when you care. The trust inside that relationship is the thing that heals. Related Article Opinion

Gender pay gap We're paid less to do so much more: one female doctor speaks out I am not alone. A study published late last year in the Australian Health Review by Professor Louise Stone, Professor Karen Price and colleagues surveyed 770 female GPs who had left or drastically reduced their clinical hours. They described themselves as an underclass, doing the profession’s invisible emotional labour for a fraction of the remuneration, and named government narratives around bulk-billing as a key driver of their exit. The authors called what these women experienced “malignant disregard”. I recognise every word. Australia faces a projected shortfall of more than 11,000 full-time-equivalent GPs by 2032. Women now make up nearly half the workforce, and we have been given a shorter expiry date. A longitudinal study of more than 4000 Australian GPs found the median age at which women left clinical practice was 47; for men, most exits came after 67. Here is what should trouble you: women were not planning to go. Mothers of young children reported lower intentions to leave than their colleagues – and left at higher rates anyway. We do not leave because we have stopped caring. We leave because we have been caring, at extraordinary personal cost, in a system that has decided not to look.

Advertisement

My patient’s children have a mother today because of a long appointment with a GP who had time to notice. That is what is being lost. Not a statistic, not a workforce number, but a particular quality of attention that keeps people out of emergency departments and out of crisis. Related Article Exclusive

Investigation Jeanne-Marie survived ‘mother of all surgeries’, but bias nearly broke her. How to fix medical misogyny I leave with profound gratitude for every patient who trusted me with their most difficult moments. They have been the privilege of my professional life. But a system that mistakes the sound of a pebble for the work of repair is not one I can afford to wait for any longer. Across Australia, female GPs are saying this out loud. I am one of them, and I will not be the last. Dr Elly Goodsall is leaving general practice after working as a GP in Newcastle since 2013. title: From Heartbreak Hill to hometown hero: Can a local star win the Sydney Marathon?
text:
Advertisement

SportAthleticsSydney Marathon From Heartbreak Hill to hometown hero: Can a local star win the Sydney Marathon? Iain Payten August 28, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Without a hint of heartbreak, Andy Buchanan recently won the City2Surf in a canter – and the experience provided two insights about his chances in the upcoming Sydney Marathon. Buchanan, who was the Australian marathon record holder until last month, is the leading local contender in the 42.195km slog on Sunday morning, which begins in North Sydney before winding through the city and out to Kingsford, then back to the Opera House. Andy Buchanan, the leading Australian male entrant in the Sydney Marathon, posing under the Harbour Bridge. Sam Mooy It is a notoriously rolling course with plenty of elevation, but Buchanan is comfortable with climbing, given his training base in Bendigo. Furthermore, the 35-year-old recently finished his preparation for the Sydney Marathon by cruising to a win over the shorter, but similarly hilly, 14km City2Surf course. “I’m really confident, the City to Surf felt quite easy and comfortable, which was a great sign,” Buchanan said. “I ran the Gold Coast Half [in July] poorly and knew I could do better, so I wanted another race to build confidence.

Advertisement

“I spoke to my coach about doing another race and he floated City to Surf. We were nervous about the hills beating my legs up three weeks out from a marathon, but the week before, I decided I really wanted to do it. So I entered that week. “I grew up in Bendigo and run hills every single day, so I’m used to it. I’m confident with hills; they don’t scare me.” Buchanan crossed the line at Bondi Beach in a time of 40 minutes, 27 seconds. It was still 23s adrift of the record set by Steve Moneghetti in 1991, who was then at the peak of his powers. The distance legend had won his first marathon in Berlin a year earlier, and remains one of only three Australians to win a Major, along with Robert DeCastella (Boston, 1986) and Lisa Ondieki, who won in New York in 1992.

Advertisement

Buchanan would love to join those Aussie icons on an elite list, but his time at the finishing gate in Bondi was a good reminder of the form required. “Moneghetti was an absolute phenomenon. I tried to beat his record a few weeks ago at City to Surf and didn’t get near it,” Buchanan said. “[Winning a major] definitely motivates me, but the running world has changed a lot from when ‘Monner’ was running. Steve Moneghetti winning the 1991 City to Surf in 40:03, which is still the record. Ben Rushton/Fairfax Media “What I love about running is that it’s so accessible—literally every country in the world runs and has access to it. Think about how many countries have a 50-metreswimming pool; probably half the world. “Whereas with running, everyone runs. The game has changed over the last five or six years. It would be an absolute fairytale to win a major, especially here in my home country, but you have to be realistic when you’re up against guys running 2:01, 2:02, or 2:03. It’s a bit different.”

Advertisement

Much has changed indeed. The marathon world record stood at 2:06:50 until 1998, but in the decades since, 448 men have officially run under that time, and the world record has been slashed by almost seven minutes. African runners now dominate distance running, with almost 90 per cent of those 448 born in Africa. Buchanan is one of two Australians in the remaining 10 per cent, with a PB of 2:06.22 set in Valencia in 2024. His time broke the national record, but it was lowered last month – just – by Haftu Strintzos, who ran a 2:06.20 on the Gold Coast. DeCastella (2:08.18 in 1981) and Moneghetti (2:08.16 in 1990) sit slightly behind in eligible PBs, but there were no supershoes in that era. Over the last decade, high-tech, energy-saving footwear has helped slash average times of elite runners by several minutes. Buchanan, a chilled-out former teacher and shoe-shop owner, has said losing his record to Strintzos felt like getting hit by “1000 cement trucks” but he is motivated to regain it. That probably won’t happen in Sydney, where fast times are tough to achieve. Wins, too, given there are 18 athletes in the Sydney field with PBs under 2:06.

Advertisement

But the race within a race in Sydney is to be the first Australian male and female finisher. The Sydney Marathon provides $30,000 prizemoney for the two Australian winners, and $20,000 and $10,000 for minor placings. It is a huge sum for cash-strapped Australian runners. “Running is a tough sport, and we don’t get the financial support that a lot of other sports get,” Buchanan said. “It’s great that the Sydney Marathon is investing back into the Australian field. For $30,000, I’m already getting into Tim [Vincent] and Liam’s [Boudin] heads, reminding them how hilly it is compared to flat Brisbane. It’s definitely a race within a race.” In the women’s field, the leading Australian contenders are Olympians Ellie Pashley, Caitlin Scott and Milly Clark.

Advertisement

Related Article Sydney Marathon Marathon, not a sprint: Why Sydney’s beast of a course rewards power over pace Pashley, a mum of two, is hitting good form after winning the Ballarat Marathon in April, and Scott showed her huge potential by winning the Melbourne marathon on debut in 2025. Clark is also a past winner of the Melbourne marathon. “I’m really excited, to be honest. I think time off from the sport really grows your hunger to get back into it,” Pashley said. “Watching last year, seeing the course, seeing the race among the Australian women, I was really pumped to try and get a spot in the race this year.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.
