title: ‘Everything shook’: Earthquake in Aussie city
text:
People living in Sydney's southwest have been left shaken today after a 3.4 magnitude earthquake struck the area.

As on Friday afternoon, just under 400 people had submitted reports of having felt the impact to the government website, with people describing feeling as though somebody had crashed into their home.

CCTV of a home in Menangle Park - shared to 7News - captured the moment the home shook.

The earthquake's epicentre is reported as having been close to Douglas Park, south of Sydney, with a depth of three kilometres.

A 3.4 magnitude earthquake has struck south of Sydney. Picture: Earthquakes@GA

According to the Geoscience Australia website, the quake struck shortly after 1pm AEST, near Appin.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The aftermath saw homeowners describe the moment shifting tectonic plates interrupted their Friday afternoons.

David Baker, who runs a Facebook page chronicling his camping trips, was watching television in his 5th floor unit n Campbelltown when the quake hit.

"I've never felt anything quite like it before," he said. "It lasted for about 10 seconds and felt like the whole block of units was shaking.

"My wife immediately said it must be an earthquake.

"Thankfully, nothing in the unit was damaged but it was definitely quite a shake."

Others posted their experiences on social media.

"I thought someone crashed into my front room, everything shook," one person wrote.

"I felt like a big gust of wind shook my house and realise (sic) there ain't no wind,"

another added.

title: Aussie hiker alive as flood nightmare unfolds
text:
An Australian woman reported missing in the Nepal floods has made contact with her parents.

Cara Severino, 26, was hiking along the Langtang Trek, in the flooding region, and was able to call her parents on Friday morning.

Australian woman, Cara Severino, made contact with her parents after devastating floods swept through the Nepal-Tibet border. feared dead has made contact with her parents from Nepal. Picture: Facebook

"We understand that they are attempting to reach Kathmandu on foot. We eagerly await more information about her safe return," her parents Debbie and Frank Severino told The Age.

"We praise God that she has been able to make this brief contact with us."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Australia's Departent of Foreign Affairs and Trade has urged the hiker to contact consular staff.

"DFAT is urgently working to get in touch with an Australian who has made contact with their family so DFAT can provide consular assistance," a spokesperson said.

"We understand that they were last reported in a remote area, several days hike from Kathmandu. DFAT is urgently engaging with local authorities on plans to assist them.

"With that Australian accounted for by their family, there are now 38 Australians unaccounted for."

Recovery will cost 'billions'

Nepal's Finance Minister says reconstructing after the landslide and floods will cost as least "a few billion dollars".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Nepal's economy is worth approximately US$45bn, compared to US$264bn in New Zealand, and $1.8 trillion for Australia.

Nepalese Finance Minister, Swarnim Wagle, told Bloomberg Television after the first phase of rescue and relief efforts, the government's second phase of recovery would potentially involve "cash for work initiatives", along with shelter, food, water, electricity and telecommunication rebuilds.

Reconstruction after the landslide is estimated to cost billions, Nepal's Finance Minister has said. Picture: NewsWire Handout/ World Vision

"Cumulatively, I think the losses and damages, when they will be finally quantified in a week or so, will amount to at least a few billion dollars," Dr Wagle said.

"Preliminary estimates are quite worrying."

Chinese President orders surveys of glaciers, lakes

Chinese President Xi Jinping has ordered faster surveys of glaciers and lakes on the Tibetan Plateau.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The President said at a meeting Friday the rescue efforts were facing "extreme difficulties", Bloomberg reports.

The comments were made at a Politburo meeting Friday, where the Chinese Communist Party's decision makers pledged assistance for Nepal and called for all-out search and rescue efforts. The Chinese government on Thursday said about 100 Chinese nationals in Nepal were unaccounted for.

A spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry said analysis had shown the destruction was likely caused by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal.

More flooding inundates areas of Nepal

Another wave of flooding is hitting inundated areas of Nepal, just days after a glacier collapsed and caused massive flash floods that have killed hundreds and left thousands missing.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The death toll now stands at 538, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority.

There are 1400 people missing – including at least 39 Australians.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities said another round of dangerous floods is threatening lives after a dam broke on the Tibetan side of the border.

The search for missing people continues in Nepal. Picture: Ezra Acayan / Getty Images

Shortly after 4pm AEST Friday, the Nepal Police issued a warning saying a barrier lake dam had broken, and that all members of the public, rescue workers and security personnel need to move to safe ground.

The alert did not appear to say which dam, village or valley was affected.

Rescue operations have been paused following the announcement.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Nepali Police confirmed the new official death toll on Friday afternoon, as local authorities warn of more potential floods, as two newly formed lakes are at risk of rising and bursting.

An injured child is treated at a field hospital inside a military camp, following flash floods on August 27, 2026 in Trishuli, Nepal. Picture: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

"Residents of the lower banks … passengers, rescuers engaged in rescue operations, and all concerned are requested to exercise special caution and stay in safe places away from the river banks and risky areas," the authority's statement read.

Those in the area have been urged to seek higher ground and move away from the river beds.

The Nepalese National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Friday morning said the lakes were forming along the Lende River, and there was a potential risk for a "huge flood" to occur.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Everyone (is) requested to adopt extreme alertness and remain with high caution. An estimation has been made that additional lakes may form in that area."

A military helicopter rescues a young man stranded by massive floods and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border. Picture: AFP

Neighbours of missing Aussies 'in shock'

A neighbour of the Iyer family, who are part of the missing cohort of Aussies, said she "slept terribly" upon realising they were caught up in the devastation.

Sreedharan Iyer, 53, Lakshmi Sreedharan Iyer, 50, and their sons Rudhra, 21, and Rishabh, 24, were travelling with US-based tour operator Himalayan Glacier Adventures at the time the natural disaster struck.

Rudhra and Rishabh are both medical students at Western Sydney University and Newcastle University respectively.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Margaret Young, 84, said she had a close relationship with Mr and Mrs Iyer, who affectionately referred to her and her husband as their "Aussie parents".

She said she had watched their two sons grow up, and the family "would do anything for you if they could".

Ms Young told NewsWire that Sreedharan had once saved her life.

"He just knew I'd had a stroke. I got an ambulance here within minutes. They took me to North Shore and did a clot retrieval, so I was super lucky that he was around," she said.

Members of the Iyer family from Sydney were last known to be in Kathmandu before the flood. Picture: Facebook

The Iyers travelled to the region with their friends, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The Iyer brothers are both studying medicine at the University of Newcastle. Rishab in his fifth year and Rudhra in his third.

Vice-Chancellor Alex Zelinsky said the nervous wait for information about the Iyer family was affecting a lot of people.

"We are thinking of them, their families, their fellow students and teaching staff, as well as the many people who have been impacted by this devastating event and we hope that both students can be located soon.

"We have more than 450 students studying with us from Nepal and many others with strong links to this region," Professor Zelinsky said.

"Our priority is supporting our students and staff during this very sad time."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Of the Australians reported missing, 15 were confirmed to be travelling with Himalayan Glacier Adventures.

Umesh and Krishna Sharma were part of the group, with their son Chitrak revealing his desperate attempts to contact his parents after learning of the disaster.

Umesh and Krishna Sharma are among at least 39 Australians reported missing. Picture: ACA

Speaking to 9News, Chitrak said the pair were "very excited" to embark on the tour.

"I've just been trying to get in contact with them … calling hospitals. I just want to find my parents. They're all I have, really," he told the broadcaster.

"I said bye to them, and I didn't think it was the last time I was ever going to see them.

"I would do anything just to bring them home."

Four members of the Muralitharan family – brothers Ashwin and Aarush Muralitharan, aged 11 and 14, and their parents Shylaja and Chandrasekaran – are on the Himalayan Glacier Adventures group list.

Satellite imagery of the flood affected areas in Nepal. Picture: X / Vantor

The floods have caused widespread destruction across parts of Nepal and China. Picture: X / Vantor

Chitra Venkatraman is missing. Picture: Supplied / ABC

Kanagamah Sundrasan is also missing. Picture: Supplied

Speaking to NewsWire, neighbour Ragu Kanagaraj said the Muralitharan family were "the kindest people I've ever met and the best neighbours anyone could ask for".

Mr Kanagaraj has been living alongside the family for 2½ years and has become close with them.

"I just hope they come back safely. I can't imagine living next to somebody else now. They've become like family to us,' he said.

He said waking up without the family next door had been heartbreaking.

"I broke down this morning. It's tough. Everything reminds me of them," he said.

"When we step outside, we see their house. It's a constant reminder."

Chandrasekaran and Shylaja Muralitharan are feared missing with their two sons Aarush and Ashwin. Picture: Supplied

Narayan Panthi, a Brisbane father of two, was also part of the group and remains unaccounted for.

"We tried to contact him and his family and friends over in Nepal – we haven't got anything back," his family friend Amrit Bhusal told 9News.

Aarush and Ashwin Muralitharan are among the Australians missing in the Nepal floods. Their parents Chandrasekaran and Shylaja Muralitharan are also missing. Picture: ACA

A group of unaccounted for missing Indian-Australian travellers, including the Muralitharan family. Picture: IndianLink

Couple Sidharthi Sahu and Sandeep Mohapatra, who were in Nepal to complete the sacred pilgrimage of Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, are also among the missing Australians.

Mr Mohapatra is an engineer and his wife, Ms Sahu, works in IT.

The couple, who moved to Australia in 2018, were part of a group heading for the sacred pilgrimage when the disaster struck.

Mr Mohapatra's cousin Soumya told the Times of India their family were fearing the worst.

"We got a call from Indian authorities saying there is no information about them," he said.

"With every passing hour, our hopes are fading."

Uday and Kripa Shivamurthy have also been named in the list of missing Australians in Nepal.

The Sydney couple, who worked as an architect and accountant respectively, were travelling with The Trekkers' Society, which specialises in tour and treks thorough Nepal, Tibet and Bhutan.

Sydney couple, Uday and Kripa Shivamurthy, were about to leave the region when the landslide and floods hit, their niece says.

The couple were known to take the pilgrimage every few years, niece Navya Nataraj told CNN.

She said the pair were returning home and waiting to cross the border from China to Nepal.

Ten minutes later, the landslide and flooding struck.

"We have been getting conflicting reports," Ms Nataraj told the outlet.

"But then today they released aerial images. We are distraught and devastated."

Outdoor Education expert Michael Keats, 37, is also among the missing.

The 41-year-old has two children and a wife in Sydney

Husband's frantic trip to disaster zone

The husband of Newcastle-based mum Reshma Patel, 46, who was near the Nepal-China border about 10 minutes before the floods tore through the region, has boarded a flight to Nepal in search of his wife.

Family friend Chin Valsan said Ms Patel was travelling home after visiting the Kailash Mansarovar as part of the Isha Foundation pilgrimage and hadn't been heard from since.

" … family and friends have been unable to reach her and are deeply concerned for her safety and wellbeing," Ms Valsan said.

She said Ms Patel's husband had boarded a flight to Nepal on Friday morning in the desperate search for his wife.

Reshma Patel was at the border of Nepal and China when the flood ripped through the region. Picture: Facebook

"If anyone has seen Reshma, has travelled with her, has information about her whereabouts or has any contacts with local authorities, hospitals, rescue teams, tour operators or pilgrimage groups in the region, please contact the family immediately or notify the nearest police authority," Ms Valsan said.

Kushagra Tiwari has been desperately trying to find out where his friend Bharat Mangwani, 42, has ended up.

Mr Tiwari told NewsWire the 42-year-old Sydney-based engineer and father of two had been on his way back from a religious pilgrimage at Lake Manasarovar when his friends and family lost contact with him.

"After that, we haven't been able to trace him. We are trying to find out any information possible," he said.

Sydney man Bharat Mangwani, 41, has not made contact with his family, and his wife Neha is travelling to Nepal to look for him, a friend tells NewsWire. Picture: Supplied

Mr Tiwari said Mr Mangwani's wife was on her way to Kathmandu to personally search for her missing husband.

Mother of two Sumi Adhikari, 41, is another Australian who was travelling with the Isha Foundation at the time of the devastating floods.

The Sydney-based Optus network engineer was at the border of Nepal and China when the floodwaters hit and hasn't been seen or heard from since.

Her husband Nava Pandey said he was flying to Nepal in search for Ms Adhikari, and urged for any information about the missing mother.

"I am in Nepal now, please only call if you have information about her," he wrote online.

Family friend Shishya Sangroula said Ms Adhikari's "last contact was from the immigration office" at the time of the flooding.

'Immense challenge' in search

Australian charities have united in the joint Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal to support those affected by the floods and landslides.

The Emergency Action Alliance is participating alongside Save the Children Australia, Plan International Australia, Oxfam Australia, Australia for UNHCR, ActionAid Australia, CARE Australia, Caritas Australia, ADRA, Act for Peace, Anglican Overseas Aid, Australian Lutheran World Service, Baptist World Aid Australia, CBM Australia, and Tearfund Australia.

EAA executive director Kerren Morris said the disaster was "heartbreaking".

"Families have lost loved ones, homes and livelihoods in a matter of hours, and many communities are now cut off from essential services," she said.

"Australians have a long history of standing alongside communities affected by disasters

around the world. This appeal brings together many of Australia's leading charities and

provides a trusted way for people to help ensure vital assistance reaches those who need it most.

The aftermath of flooding in Rasuwa. Picture: NewsWire Handout/ World Vision

"Emergency shelter, food, safe drinking water and medical support are urgently needed now, while longer-term recovery efforts will continue for many months."

The Australian arm of Catholic charity Caritas is also directing funds and efforts to the Emergency Action Alliance.

Caritas humanitarian manager Sally Thomas said Caritas Nepal workers delivering aid into the affected regions were doing so under the threat of more flooding, particularly in Nuwakot.

"Humanitarians often work in incredibly dangerous circumstances, and those most in danger are almost always local people supporting their own communities," she said.

Caritas Nepal had set up a kitchen to feed 300 families over the next 15 days, and handed out tarps, mats and blankets to try and stop people sleeping outside from succumbing to wet weather.

"Beyond eating and finding somewhere dry to sleep, communities also require support to keep themselves and their families clean, access medical support for any injuries sustained as well as ongoing conditions," Ms Thomas said.

" … which is particularly acute for the elderly or pregnant, as well as mental health support as people are understandably incredibly traumatised.

"This trauma is being compounded by the fear of another wall of water heading their way."

Aid workers are particularly concentrated on hard-hit Nuwakot. Picture: NewsWire handout / World Vision

On Friday morning, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said officials were working urgently to confirm the welfare of the missing Australians and provide assistance to those affected.

"The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery," she said.

"The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is deploying additional personnel to support Australians affected by the disaster."

Senator Wong said Australia would send $5m in humanitarian assistance, including $2m for the World Food Program to dispatch food rations and logistics support.

Australia will provide $2m to Australian NGOs through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership, offering emergency shelter, hygiene kits, blankets, medical support and psychosocial support, and a further $1m to the Emergency Action Alliance to support local-led recovery and rehabilitation in the impacted regions.

More than 1400 people remain unaccounted for. Picture: Supplied / AFP

Speaking to ABC Radio National, Senator Wong said it was an "awful disaster" and authorities were working to identify how many Australians were in the region at the time.

She said a further four Australians remain unaccounted for, bringing the total to 39.

"Yesterday we knew of 35 (missing Australians), we know an additional four were travelling separately to these tours," she said.

"We have been contacting families of the unaccounted for."

Victoria's Multicultural Affairs Minister, Paul Edbrooke, said the government would do anything it could to help Nepalese Australians.

"The Nepali community is one of the fastest growing in Victoria. We stand with you in your moment of pain.

"If there is anything the Victorian government can do to support your community through this period, we will."

"The loss is heartbreaking … We commend the efforts of emergency services and volunteers in Nepal and China, who are working tirelessly."

DFAT personnel have been deployed to the region and are assisting with crisis response.

There are 5400 members of the Nepali Army taking part in the rescue and providing medical assistance to the more than 900 people injured.

The Nepali Army said they had rescued 200 people from the ground and evacuated nearly 700 others, including 101 foreign nationals, via helicopter.

The Indian air force has been deployed to assist with the provision of supplies and rescuing survivors.

Senator Wong said Australia would deploy further assistance to the region to assist the families of those unaccounted for.

"It's a very difficult situation, it's a remote location," she said.

Hundreds of Nepalese Australians have contacted the Australian government hoping for information about their loved ones, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong says. Picture: NewsWire / Emma Brasier

She told ABC Radio Adelaide the department were working to contact the next of kin for the 39 missing Australians.

"We've had over 300 calls since we opened the centre yesterday and we are making calls and contacting next of kin when we can identify … the Australians who are currently missing."

She issued a message to the families of those affected by the disaster.

"I know this is an extremely distressing time," she said.

"For those who have loved ones unaccounted for, our thoughts are with them."

Tour company Intrepid told NewsWire it operated 26 itineraries in Nepal, with two passing through the affected region.

However, none of the tours were operating at the time of the flood, the company said.

"For travellers with upcoming bookings to Nepal, we recommend staying in contact with their tour operator for the latest information relevant to their itinerary," a spokesman said.

"While the flooding has had a devastating impact on communities in parts of the Langtang and Trishuli River region, the majority of Intrepid's Nepal itineraries are operating as planned and have not been affected."

Commercial flights to Nepal continue

Senator Wong told ABC Radio Adelaide that commercial flights would still operate in and out of Nepal as the search for those missing continues.

"Commercial flights are still available was the advice I had this morning," she said.

"I think everyone would be aware of the catastrophic situation that the Nepalese people and Nepalese authorities are dealing with right now."

Smartraveller has advised those travelling in Nepal as part of a group or tour to contact the operator or travel agent for updates and support.

"If you're in an affected area, monitor local media for updates, follow the advice of local authorities, avoid floodwaters, landslide-prone areas and damaged infrastructure, review your travel plans and allow extra time for disruptions," the website read.

"Transport services in the area may be disrupted or cancelled, including flights and buses.

"Contact your transport provider to confirm your service is running before going to the airport or station."

title: Missing Aussie makes contact as flood disaster worsens
text:
Australian authorities are urgently trying to reach a woman who made contact with family after surviving catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-China border.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is engaging with local authorities on plans to assist the woman, who is understood to have been last reported in a remote area several days' hike from Kathmandu.

At least 38 Australians remain missing after an ice avalanche on Wednesday triggered Nepal's worst natural disaster in more than a decade.

Australia is sending humanitarian workers to help with disaster recovery efforts. (Suryams Upreti/AAP PHOTOS)

Heavy continued rainfall is making rescue conditions difficult and unpredictable.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Further severe flooding, landslides and debris flows are predicted in the affected areas of Nepal and Tibet while a lake formed by the landslide has started to overflow.

At least 489 people have died, Nepalese authorities said, while almost 1000 remain missing.

Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was on a pilgrimage on the China-Nepal border when the catastrophic flash flooding hit.

Her husband Kailash Mansowar, who has not heard from her since, has travelled to the region from Sydney to find her, guided only by her iPhone's last location.

"I am here in Nepal now (since) yesterday and working with local authorities to find further information," he told AAP on Friday.

Sumi Adhikari is among the Australians missing following deadly floods in Nepal and Tibet. (PR IMAGE PHOTO)

Like many missing Australians, Ms Adhikari was undertaking a group tour, in her case with the Isha Foundation.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She left Kathmandu on August 14 after flying from Sydney to trek to a sacred site near Tibet's Mount Kailash.

"Even the smallest piece of information could help bring her home," a widely shared post on social media announcing her disappearance reads.

A separate group of 15 Australians, including two boys aged 11 and 14, were travelling with US-based tourism operator Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company.

Authorities in China and Nepal say further flooding could complicate local rescue efforts. (AP PHOTO)

Sydney doctor Manoj Dharmaratnam, who was invited to join the sacred pilgrimage but chose not to go, prescribed several of his friends altitude medication and conducted injury assessments before they left Australia.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"One of them had an injury and I did tell her, maybe you're not fit to go on this trek," Dr Dharmaratnam told AAP.

"She actually called up and cancelled her trip ... but then she said I've bought the ticket, so I might as well go."

The Himalayan Glacier group included a well-respected Sydney couple with two sons in their 20s, both studying medicine in NSW, he said.

At least four Australians were travelling separately to tour groups, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Friday.

Sydney doctor Manoj Dharmaratnam declined an invitation for the pilgrimage. (Dan Himbrechts/AAP PHOTOS)

Senator Wong said the federal government would send additional personnel to the region and unveiled a $5 million assistance package and humanitarian support.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

An initial team of three humanitarian response specialists will be sent to help 20 staff already on the ground in Nepal.

But Chinese and Nepalese authorities say local rescue efforts could be complicated by further flooding, caused by a build-up of debris.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Thursday (AEST) warned a lake was forming above the Rasuwagadhi border.

By Friday it had begun to overflow.

Search and rescue operations are still under way in the debris-strewn areas of Nepal. (AP PHOTO)

The Lhendi River had been obstructed about 18 kilometres above the border, posing a risk to residents in areas below, it said in a statement on social media.

The threat of a second flood caused by a blockage upstream led to evacuation orders at Jilong Port on the Nepal-China border, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Rocks, boulders and debris lodged in the valley, as well as lakes forming along the plateau, could cause further flooding, geoscientist Jakob Steiner told AAP.

"Unfortunately it's not over ... this material is only going to lie there. We cannot move it away," Dr Steiner, a fellow at the Asian Mountain Alliance, said.

"Every time a new flood comes, it's going to move this, and this is just going to increase future flood events in terms of impact."

As local communities await news, more disaster response specialists are being sent to Nepal. (George Chan/AAP PHOTOS)

A candlelight vigil for Nepalese-Australians will be held on the front lawns of Parliament House in Canberra on Friday night.

Similar ceremonies were held in Sydney and Melbourne on Thursday.

Australians who need urgent help should contact DFAT's 24-hour consular emergency centre.

title: ‘Humoured him’: Perrottet brother on Nassif
text:
A brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet has told a corruption inquiry he knew fugitive property developer Jean Nassif wanted to build influence inside the Liberal Party.

Charles Perrottet told the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption he tried to keep the developer onside for his own reasons.

He said Mr Nassif often rang him directly to complain about his projects and figures including former minister David Elliott.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I wanted to appease him. I humoured him at times because I had an ulterior motive to seek some information from him in regard to allegations that had been around," Charles Perrottet said in evidence on Friday.

He also told the inquiry he helped chase unpaid Beckington invoices and gave Mr Nassif updates about activity inside the Liberal Party, while insisting "what I said to Jean Nassif was very different to my actions in the party".

The ICAC is investigating whether fugitive developer Mr Nassif made illegal donations to Liberal Party figures in return for help advancing his interests, including efforts to remove former building commissioner David Chandler from office and damage the political career of former minister David Elliott.

Dominic Perrottet, Mr Elliott and Mr Chandler are not accused of any wrongdoing.

Charles Perrottet began giving his evidence in the ICAC corruption inquiry. Picture: NewsWire / Nikki Shor

Wife's second day of evidence

Charles Perrottet's wife Alice earlier on Friday spend a second day in the witness box at the ICAC.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She was pressed over nearly $661,000 paid into her company, disputed travel claims and a detailed email about Mr Nassif and Toplace as an ICAC corruption inquiry intensifies.

Anita Perrottet returned to the witness box on Friday, while her husband Charles Perrottet began his evidence late in the day and will resume on Monday.

Ms Perrottet first gave evidence on Wednesday when she was questioned about payments to her company, her business dealings and what she knew of her husband's political work.

She is not a person of interest in the ICAC hearing.

Money and records

A major focus was the money paid into Ms Perrottet's company, Macquarie Consulting, from Beckington and JPG Advisory.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC told the inquiry the total amount received over about two and a half years was roughly $661,000, despite Ms Perrottet maintaining there was no written work product because her advice was verbal.

"That's an enormous amount of money to be paid for circumstances where you cannot produce a scrap of evidence in relation to work done," Ms Dwyer told her.

Ms Perrottet stood by her evidence that the work was genuine and oral.

Anita and Charles Perrottet (left and centre) gave evidence at ICAC on Friday over Liberal Party donations. Picture: NewsWire / Nikki Short

'The game is exposed'

Ms Perrottet was shown an email she purportedly sent to Jeremy Greenwood in March 2023 sharing documents relating to work for Greyhound Racing NSW, despite her earlier evidence that the work was entirely verbal.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The email was sent after a parliamentary inquiry had begun examining the activities of Liberal Party figures, including Mr Greenwood and Charles Perrottet.

The commission was told Ms Perrottet had also created a shared drive of Greyhound Racing NSW material.

Ms Perrottet told the inquiry she could not remember creating the documents or what was in them.

"That is a completely sham email suggesting an arrangement where you're swapping or sharing greyhound docs that did not exist, isn't it?" Ms Dwyer said.

Ms Perrottet replied: "No."

"Oh, Mrs Perrottet, the game is exposed, isn't it? It is just completely ludicrous to maintain the position that you have, that this was a genuine business," Ms Dwyer said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Ms Perrottet responded: "It was a genuine business."

Ms Dwyer then put to her that the evidence she had given "is patently false".

Ms Perrottet replied: "I'm sorry, I had forgotten about these. I don't remember."

Anita Perrottet returned to the witness box on Friday at the ICAC corruption inquiry. Picture: ICAC

Texts on power

A series of messages shown to ICAC placed Ms Perrottet squarely inside conversations about the Liberal Party's internal power struggles as Dominic Perrottet moved into the premiership.

In one exchange, Charles Perrottet told his wife he had a "long call with Dom" and that his brother had thanked him "for everything, not just this weekend, but the last 20 years to get here".

Later, after Ms Perrottet asked whether David Elliott would miss out on a ministry, Charles replied: "I didn't ask … We execute the prick as soon as party room is over."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Asked if there was any other way to read that message other than as a reference to Mr Elliott, Ms Perrottet told the inquiry she was not sure what it meant.

David Elliott is not accused of wrongdoing.

Travel claims questioned

The inquiry then turned to flights, hotels, parking, Ubers and other costs claimed through Macquarie Consulting in late 2021 and early 2022.

Ms Perrottet struggled to explain a series of Sydney expenses and accepted some may have been "an oversight" or "an error".

"If I came to Sydney and I recorded it like this, it would have been a combination of family and work," she told the commission.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Ms Dwyer repeatedly put to her that some of the claimed Sydney expenses appeared to match Charles Perrottet's travel rather than her own, including dates when text messages showed he was in Sydney and she was in Melbourne.

Ms Perrottet did not accept that her husband was claiming work expenses through her company.

Jean Nassif is expected to give evidence to the inquiry by video link on Friday next week. Picture: NSW Police

Toplace email revealed

The inquiry also homed in on an October 2020 email sent from Ms Perrottet's Macquarie Consulting account to lobbying firm Premier National about a Toplace development in Rosebery.

The email referred to owners wanting to "commence action against Jean for noncompliance due to not having the OC in place" and set out detailed project and planning issues.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Ms Dwyer pointed out that Ms Perrottet had previously told the inquiry she did not work for Toplace, did not work for Mr Nassif and did not know the project belonged to Toplace.

"You've told us up until this time, Mrs Perrottet, that you did not work for Toplace, you did not work for Jean Nassif, you did not know that this was a development owned by Toplace, and here I'm showing you a detailed email where you are advocating in relation to Toplace and Jean Nassif," Ms Dwyer said.

Lunch and politics

Ms Perrottet was shown messages sent to her husband before the lunch, including one suggesting "you should look up a wine to buy and take on Saturday", along with another on the day referring to her being too sick to attend.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Asked whether that refreshed her memory that the plan had been for her and Charles to attend lunch with the children at Mr Nassif's home, she replied: "No, I don't remember that at all."

She was later shown photographs of her children playing at the home.

Asked whether that prompted any memory that Charles and the children had been there, Ms Perrottet replied: "No, I'm sorry."

Peggy Dwyer SC pressed Ms Perrottet over disappearing messages and her recollection of a lunch involving Mr Nassif. Picture: ICAC

The inquiry was also shown a text exchange between Ms Perrottet and her husband that touched on Liberal Party branch politics.

In one message, Charles Perrottet mentioned veteran conservative Liberal figure David Clarke and the Beecroft branch before adding, "Sorry that was for Christian."

Ms Perrottet replied, "Your other lover." In another, she wrote: "time to kill Clarke, isn't he like 305 years old?"

Ms Dwyer suggested the exchange showed Ms Perrottet did discuss her husband's political work with him.

Ms Perrottet replied: "I appreciate that from this text exchange it looks like that, but for me, it's one of probably hundreds of millions of text exchanges with my husband."

title: Caravanners blown away by Aussie boy's simple gesture 'in the middle of nowhere'
text:
Heading north through the Northern Territory, caravanner Eleni and her husband didn't expect that a roadside pile of rocks would leave such an impact on them and the wider community.

A simple gesture by an 11-year-old boy named Flynn "in the middle of nowhere" has become "such a positive experience for so many people," the traveller told Yahoo News Australia.

Pulling into a free camp just outside Timber Creek in the Northern Territory this week, they thought nothing of the simple pit stop listed as Ferdinand Von Mueller's Gravel Pit on WikiCamps.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

But there it was, a pile of rocks carefully arranged into a fire pit, which immediately changed how people viewed the humble patch of gravel.

"When we pulled over, my hubby saw the rocks and went over to it," Eleni said.

Do you have a travelling story? Contact

Eleni Pringle and her husband discovered the fire pit when they visited the free campsite this week. (Eleni Pringle)

What did Flynn's campfire note say?

Next to it was a note written by Flynn, a young boy travelling around Australia with his twin brother and their parents.

He'd built the fire pit rock by rock during his stay there with his family days earlier. And as he left, he vowed to offer it up for fellow travellers passing through.

RELATED:

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

On the red dirt beneath the circle of rocks, a note read: "I made this fireplace, and you can use it too. This is for everyone. Please don't destroy it."

Young Flynn marked the date, 14th August 2026, and asked visitors to "please write the date of the day you see this on the back".

Flynn left a note beside the fire pit inviting othres to use it. (Eleni Pringle)

Flynn asked fellow travellers to write teh date they stayed at the camp. Already, his fire pit has been used by several campers. (Eleni Pringle)

When Eleni arrived, several people had already left their mark. They too used the fire and marked the date.

Among those who signed the paper were travellers from England, Germany and the small Queensland town of Imbil.

"It was really cool to find it in such an odd spot in the middle of nowhere. We put it in a plastic sleeve as well to protect it from the weather," she said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I just thought it was such a cool little thing for someone to do. And I thought he needs to see what he's put out there."

Caravanner tracks down Flynn's family using social media

Touched by the gesture, Eleni felt compelled to share it online with the wider community. They hoped to find Flynn and let him know that people are using his fire pit.

Within an hour of posting in a Facebook group designed for travellers, word got to Flynn's mum, Jade McInnes, and in less than 24 hours, the post has garnered almost 6,000 likes.

The Ferdinand Von Mueller free campsite in the Northern Territory has been renamed on WikiCamps to 'Flynn's Fire Pit'. (WikiCamps/Supplied)

Family reveals how Flynn's fire pit came about

Flynn's dad, Sam, told Yahoo his son is blown away by the response he's received.

Sam said they never expected the simple gesture to make such an impact. And they certainly didn't expect so many people to use the pit.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It's been really rewarding for him. He was pretty chuffed," Sam said.

The family, from Western Australia, had visited the fee campsite on August 14th.

Normally, they use an arc pit — a little stainless-steel fire pit that's quite popular with caravanners — but on this particular night, they decided to make a bush fire pit out of rocks.

Flynn is travelling in northern Australia in a caravan with his twin brother and their parents, Sam and Jade. (Jade McInnes)

"He got pretty excited," Sam said. "I was just going to do a single layer, but he kept going.

"He was going in and out of the bush, bringing out rocks like a little stonemason. He kept wanting to build it higher and higher.

"When we were leaving, he goes, 'oh, I'm going to leave a note so that all the people staying here can enjoy it as well'."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Sam said, "It was all 100 per cent his idea to leave a note".

Flynn was thrilled to make a fire pit himself, with his dad Sam describing how excited his son was. (Jade McInnes)

He added it was "quite funny to watch" and "pretty cute" to see his son so proud of the fire pit he was creating. And it's "great to see" it's resonated with so many people online, too.

Especially since, in the days that followed, he broke his foot in a mountain bike accident, making him feel "a little bit down in the dumps".

"He's a pretty modest young fella, I don't quite think he realises how many people he's actually touched through such a simple task," the proud dad said.

"It's just great to see that social media is being used for something positive nowadays. It's a refreshing change."
